issues.body:
## TL;DR

Complete the 280-policy Delphi TPP40 two-phase swarm across East5 and Europe. Twenty-seven East5 policies are complete. The frozen candidate assignment gives East5 126 policies, including two resumable phase-boundary checkpoints, and Europe 127 fresh policies. Production launch remains gated on one paired cross-accelerator trajectory with absolute BPB differences at most 0.002 for phase-boundary Uncheatable, endpoint Uncheatable, and endpoint Table 9.

## Description

The original East5-only parent made slow progress because v5p-8 capacity was scarce. The multiregion plan uses region-local datasets, validation caches, state, checkpoints, and evaluations. It does not transfer training corpora across regions. East5 keeps the 27 completed and two resumable lineages; Europe receives disjoint fresh policies and trains on v6e-8.

The assignment covers all 280 run orders exactly once. A content-addressed path audit resolved all 153 East-assigned lineages: 27 completed rows have successful executor status and final artifacts, rows 27 and 29 have permanent phase-boundary checkpoints, and 124 rows are fresh. Europe production remains blocked until run order 2 passes the paired numerical and idempotence gate.

## Hypothesis or Goal

Complete the preregistered TPP40 panel without changing its policies or training configuration, while accepting only cross-accelerator differences that remain within the frozen 0.002 BPB paired threshold.

## Status

The Europe bridge trajectory for run order 2 is training. The production assignment and commands have passed locality and dry-run checks but are provisional until the bridge gate passes. After acceptance, the assignment will be re-materialized and required to retain byte-identical and semantic hashes before the East5 and Europe parents are submitted.

## Links

* Logbook: https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/calvin/swarm-olmo3-regmix-test/.agents/logbooks/delphi-tpp40-multiregion.md
* Fieldbook: `exp_01kz3nq7y7mp3a51kz26cvv4tr`
* W&B Report: pending
* Important updates: pending

## Decision Log

* 2026-08-30: Use one paired trajectory, run order 2, as the production bridge gate. East5 evaluation capacity may delay the paired result but does not authorize an unpaired launch.
* 2026-08-30: Keep all datasets and mutable artifacts region-local. Do not use Storage Transfer Service or copy training corpora across regions.
* 2026-08-30: Freeze a disjoint 126-row East5 and 127-row Europe assignment after accounting for 27 completed East5 rows.

## Conclusion

Pending the run-order-2 bridge gate and production launch.

issues.author: yonromai
issues.body:
A weekly GPU vLLM refresh currently reserves accelerators in two places. The
vLLM release flow validates the exact x86_64 and aarch64 candidate wheels
through Iris on H100 and GB200. Marin then validates the same candidate with a
Snowball output comparison and a bounded Qwen3 serving test on H100. Both H100
gates install the candidate wheel and exercise a live serving path.

Move accelerator qualification for a GPU wheel candidate into the Marin
refresh. The vLLM workflow should build immutable x86_64 and aarch64 candidate
wheels without reserving an accelerator. Marin should qualify those exact
wheel bytes on H100 and GB200, run the Snowball and Qwen3 integration checks,
and record one result that binds the source commit, wheel URLs and digests, and
both hardware results. H100 and GB200 remain required because they test
different architecture-specific wheels.

[#7995](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/7995) records the
current two-architecture release gate and immutable-wheel promotion. It does
not explain why the later Marin H100 test is a separate gate.

Done when:

- Building a GPU wheel candidate does not reserve an accelerator.
- Marin tests the exact x86_64 wheel on H100 and the exact aarch64 wheel on
  GB200. The qualification preserves the current install, native-extension,
  runtime, and serving checks needed to catch wheel or architecture failures.
- One result identifies the source commit, wheel URLs and digests, H100 and
  GB200 results, and the Marin Snowball and Qwen3 results.
- A failed or missing hardware result blocks promotion.
- Promotion reuses the qualified wheel bytes without rebuilding them.
- Ordinary fork PR CI, scheduled nightlies, and the TPU release flow are
  unchanged.

cc @rjpower
issues.title: [vllm] Move GPU refresh qualification into Marin

issues.author: penfever
issues.body: A series of experiments on the [Leonardo](https://www.hpc.cineca.it/systems/hardware/leonardo/) cluster plumbing [MarinSkyRL](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL). Aim is to optimize throughput for *non-agentic* tasks ... Leonardo is in principle viable for agentic rollouts as well, but because of the rotating keys, no-internet-on-compute-node limitation and limited VRAM per node (A100 64GB) it is expected that Jupiter, MareNostrum, EmpireAI and potentially Iris TPU will be preferred for agentic.

comments.author: penfever
comments.body:
## Leonardo non-agentic RL throughput results — gsm8k GRPO (short) + MATH (long-CoT)

Results from the MarinSkyRL throughput ablations on Leonardo. Methodology is "measure the per-step timing breakdown from the run logs, sweep one knob at a time, compare on **effective tokens/s** for work-changing cells and **sec/step** for work-fixed cells."

### Constraints & hparams

**Hardware / stack**
- CINECA Leonardo, **A100-64GB** (4/node; NVLink intra-node, InfiniBand inter-node). 64 GB/GPU is the binding VRAM limit; no compute-node internet; rotating keys.
- MarinSkyRL (`skyrl-train`): FSDP2 policy + vLLM rollout, **`colocate_all=true`**, `run_engines_locally=true`, NCCL policy→engine weight sync, `use_kl_loss=false`. Synchronous path (gen and train do **not** overlap).

**gsm8k grid base** — Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct, GRPO. Canary: `train_batch_size=32` · `n_samples_per_prompt=4` · `gpu_memory_utilization=0.70` · `enforce_eager=true` · 4 engines × TP1 · `micro_*_batch_size_per_gpu=8` · `max_generate_length=512`. Reference: **9.58 s/step** (233-step epoch).

**MATH (long-CoT) base** — Hendrycks MATH L3–5 (5,582 train) + MATH-500 val; Minerva boxed-answer **±1 reward**; `train_batch_size=64` · `n_samples=4` · `max_generate_length=4096` · CUDA graphs ON. Natural CoT (~600–660 tok), no forced EOS.

**Protocol** — 25-step runs; warm-mean over steps 6–25 (first 5 discarded). Reward is *not* converged at 25 steps, so **entropy stability** (~0.36, no collapse everywhere) is the correctness guard, not absolute reward.

### gsm8k 1.5B throughput grid (18 cells)

- **CUDA graphs (`enforce_eager=false`) is the standout near-free win: −29% sec/step (9.61 → 6.81), generation −50% (5.73 → 2.89 s).** Should be ON always.
- **Wider rollout batch (`train_batch_size` × `n_samples`) scales effective tokens/s** by filling the otherwise-starved generator. Best balance: `combo_C` (tbs128·n8·gmu0.85·cudagraph·micro16) = **12,882 eff tok/s @ 20.7 s/step**. Max throughput: `max_width` (tbs512…) = **15,231 eff tok/s** but 70.7 s/step.
- **The bottleneck MIGRATES with width.** At base width the canary is **generation-bound (gen 60%) AND the generator is starved** (KV cache usage 0.0–0.3%, "Running" 1–6 of a 1.3M-token cache). Beyond ~tbs128, **`policy_train` compute becomes the wall** (tbs256 50%, combo_D 56%, max_width 58%) while generation stays ~6–16 s and KV stays <11%. It is **never memory-bound** (max_width peaked 10.2% KV; the only "ceiling" was *dataset exhaustion* — epochs=1 × 7,473 rows ÷ tbs512 = 14 steps).
- **Layout:** 4×TP1 > 2×TP2 > 1×TP4 for the 1.5B; colocated > disaggregated at 4 GPU.

### Multi-node generator scaling (batch fixed at 2,048 seqs; scale engines = 4×nodes)

| nodes | engines | sec/step | gen-frac | policy_train-frac | sync_weights s | eff tok/s |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 4 | 36.9 | 24.3% | 55.7% | 1.05 | 14,435 |
| 2 | 8 | 73.7 | 8.6% | 68.4% | 2.40 | 7,222 |
| 4 | 16 | 46.6 | 10.5% | 62.1% | 3.63 | 11,394 |
| 8 | 32 | 35.9 | 12.3% | 51.1% | 6.33 | 14,838 |

**gsm8k/1.5B is never generation-bound — zero extra engines help.** 1→2 nodes is a sharp regression (cross-node FSDP all-gather/reduce-scatter on a tiny 1.5B doesn't amortize); 8 nodes only *breaks even* with 1 node. New monotonic limiter at scale = `sync_weights` (NCCL broadcast grows with engine count).

### Model-size saturation on a real long-CoT task (MATH), single node 4×A100-64GB

| model | parallelism | sec/step | gen-frac | policy_train-frac | avg gen tok | reward (±1) | OOM? |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1.5B | FSDP4 + 4×TP1 | 28.3 | **0.52** | 0.35 | 609 | −0.95 (~2% pass) | ok |
| 3B | FSDP4 + 4×TP1 | 41.7 | 0.47 | 0.40 | 663 | −0.81 | ok |
| 7B | FSDP4 + 4×TP1 | 68.4 | 0.45 | 0.42 | 659 | −0.13 | ok |
| 14B | FSDP4 + 2×TP2 | 100.9 | **0.32** | **0.53** | 612 | ~0.00 (~50% pass) | ok |
| 32B | FSDP4 + 1×TP4 | — | — | — | — | — | **OOM ceiling** |

- **Direction flip vs the naive guess:** on a real long-CoT task the **small end is generation-bound** (1.5B gen-frac 0.52) — opposite of short-gsm8k. As size grows the system becomes **more train-bound** (FSDP fwd+bwd scales superlinearly with params); **crossover is 7B↔14B**.
- Reward rises monotonically with size (~2% → ~50% MATH pass). **32B OOMs single-node** (cleared vLLM init but OOM'd in the FSDP backward) → needs multi-node / disaggregated.

### Bigger models, multi-node (MATH)
- **Qwen3-32B (dense): TRAINS on 2 nodes / 8 GPU** — FSDP (cpu_offload + gradient_checkpointing), vLLM 4×TP2 (TP1 OOMs), gmu 0.75, `max_model_len=8192`. ~1,534 s/step, **policy_train 71%** (gen-frac **0.19** — the train-bound trend continues: 1.5B 0.52 → 14B 0.32 → 32B 0.19).
- **Qwen3-30B-A3B (MoE):** EP trainer path works end-to-end (grouped-GEMM + router-replay; `torchtitan` installed, zero stack conflict), but OOMs at the colocated full-weight `broadcast_to_inference_engines` → also needs multi-node / disaggregated weight-sync.

### Context-length stress (Qwen2.5-7B; workload fixed at prompt 1024 / gen 4096; only `max_model_len` grows)

| max_model_len | vLLM max-concurrency | sec/step | gen-frac | KV% pk | OOM? |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 16k | 38.9× | 68.6 | 0.46 | 4.2 | ok |
| 32k | 19.5× | 71.4 | 0.47 | 4.1 | ok |
| 65k | 9.7× | 69.8 | 0.47 | 4.2 | ok |
| 131k | 4.9× | 70.5 | 0.47 | 4.1 | ok |

**No context ceiling to 131k on 4×A100-64GB** (KV pool constant ~638k tok / 34 GiB @ gmu 0.85; max-concurrency halves cleanly per doubling; throughput flat ~70 s/step). **Caveat:** this is a KV-*capacity* test — the ~660-tok CoT never fills the window; a true long-context test needs a long-**input** task (repo-level / long-doc), where realized concurrency would collapse toward ~1 and the actual ceiling would appear.

### Takeaways for Leonardo non-agentic RL
1. **Single-node throughput recipe:** `enforce_eager=false` + `gpu_memory_utilization=0.85` + wide batch (tbs128–256 × n8) + `micro_train_batch_size_per_gpu=16` → ~13–15k eff tok/s at 1.5B. (Raise `epochs` for wide-tbs so runs aren't capped by dataset exhaustion.)
2. **Generation-boundedness is a function of (model size, CoT length), not batch alone:** small models + long CoT → generation dominates (added generators pay off); large models / short outputs → train-bound (levers are train-side micro-batch/sharding + the structural **fully-async** overlap, which is the biggest untapped win and not yet exploited here).
3. **64 GB/GPU is the real ceiling** for ≥32B colocated long-context RL → multi-node / disaggregated (offload inference off the training GPUs).

comments.author: penfever
comments.body:
🤖 *(posted by an agent on behalf of @penfever)*

## OPD grid results — on-policy distillation (Qwen3-32B teacher → Qwen3-1.7B student), gsm8k, Leonardo

Companion to the pure-RL throughput grid above. **OPD** = on-policy distillation: the student (Qwen3-1.7B) generates rollouts via vLLM; per-token reward = −KL(student‖teacher) over the student's own tokens (`advantage_estimator=no_op`, `policy_loss_type=importance_sampling`, `use_kl_in_reward=true`). FSDP ref worker = KL teacher; a separate vLLM-served **Qwen3-32B** supplies top-K logprobs. No env reward. Non-agentic, local gsm8k parquet. Base: 2 nodes × 4 A100-64GB, teacher TP2 + student 1.7B FSDP2 + 4× colocated vLLM TP1.

**Structural finding:** OPD is **teacher-score-bound — 90–97% of every step** is the 32B teacher scoring rollout tokens (`prompt_logprobs=top_k` over every response token). Student generate (8–24 s) and train (38–91 s) are noise. So the speed levers all act on teacher scoring; convergence is governed separately by lr.

### Batch 1 — speed (one knob off base; warm-mean steps 5–15)
| cell | knob vs base | sec/step | teacher-score % | KL Δ (run) | note |
|---|---|--:|--:|--:|---|
| **base** | topk128·lr1e-5·tbs64·n8·gen1024·TP2·eager | 1461 | 95.7% | −0.022 | reference |
| **topk32** | top_k=32 | **532** | 89.5% | −0.023 | **2.74× faster, KL-Δ unharmed** |
| topk64 | top_k=64 | 834 | 93.0% | **−0.028** | best Batch-1 KL-Δ |
| topk256 | top_k=256 | 2663 | 97.3% | −0.018 | 1.82× slower, *worst* total Δ |
| teacherTP4 | teacher TP4 | 1401 | 95.5% | −0.026 | ≈ base — teacher scoring not TP-bound (non-lever) |
| tbs128 | train_batch=128 | 2899 | 95.9% | −0.030 | ~2× tokens → ~2× wall; eff tok/s flat (anti-lever) |
| gen512 | max_gen=512 | 796 | 93.9% | −0.036 | −46% step (halves scored tokens); diff operating point |
| cudagraph | enforce_eager=false | 1446 | 95.8% | −0.027 | no win (student gen <2% of step) |

**top_k is THE speed knob** (superlinear: each doubling ≈1.6–1.85× cost) **and convergence does not scale with it** — k=32–64 captures the bulk of teacher mass for this pair, so cheap top_k loses ~nothing in KL descent. teacherTP4 / cudagraph are non-levers here; tbs128 is anti. Entropy healthy everywhere (0.18→0.29–0.35, no collapse).

### Batch 2 — convergence (one knob off base; 8h wall ≈16 steps)
| cell | lr | n_samp | steps | KL first→last (Δ) | pass@k last | sec/step | note |
|---|--:|--:|--:|---|--:|--:|---|
| lr3e6 | 3e-6 | 8 | 16 | 0.357→0.337 (−0.020) | p@8 **0.03** | 1428 | lr too low — no task learning (≈ base lr1e-5) |
| **lr3e5** | 3e-5 | 8 | 16 | 0.357→0.313 (**−0.043**) | p@8 **0.75** | 1417 | **WINNER** — pass@8 0.03→0.75; entropy/grad healthy |
| lr1e4 | 1e-4 | 8 | 16 | 0.357→**5.59** (+5.23) | p@8 0.39 | 1415 | **diverges** (KL spike 19, grad 21) — too aggressive |
| n4 | 1e-5 | 4 | 16 | 0.366→0.334 (−0.031) | p@4 0.34 | **723** | cheapest (2× steps/hr), higher-variance, still descends |
| n16 | 1e-5 | 16 | 10/12 ⛔TIMEOUT | 0.360→0.343 (−0.017) | p@16 0.59 | 2843 | lowest-variance; killed by 8h wall (partial accepted) |

**lr — not top_k — is the dominant convergence lever; knee at lr=3e-5.** Batch-1's flat KL descent + stuck pass@8 (~0.03) was an lr=1e-5 artifact: at lr=3e-5 the *same* config doubles KL-Δ and lifts gsm8k pass@8 0.03→0.75 (first cell to actually learn the task). lr=3e-6 ≈ no movement; lr=1e-4 diverges. lr and top_k are **orthogonal** (lr = whether it converges; top_k = teacher-mass fidelity per second).

### combo_opt — confirmation (`lr=3e-5 · top_k=64 · n8 · gen1024`, 16 steps)
- **pass@8 0.75–0.78** — matches the lr3e-5 winner (full convergence)
- **KL Δ ≈ −0.05** — best clean KL-Δ of the whole grid
- **832 s/step — ~1.7× faster** than the lr3e-5 cell (topk128, 1417 s/step), entropy healthy 0.30

Confirms orthogonality: top_k=64 keeps lr3e-5's convergence at 1.7× the speed.

### Recommended production OPD config (grid closed 2026-06-07)
**`lr=3e-5 · top_k=64 · n_samples=8 · gen=1024 · teacher TP2 · cudagraph off`** → gsm8k pass@8 ~0.75–0.78, KL-Δ ~−0.05, ~832 s/step (2 nodes / 8×A100). lr is the dominant convergence lever (knee at 3e-5), top_k=32–64 the cheap near-lossless speed lever, n_samples a clean speed×variance trade.

comments.author: penfever
comments.body:
🤖 *(posted by an agent on behalf of @penfever)*

## Analysis — best RL vs best OPD (RESOLVED by the cross-grids)

> **Updated 2026-06-08.** This supersedes the original "RL has only a throughput result, the comparison is still owed" framing. The two cross-grids — [RL accuracy + OPD throughput](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/6218#issuecomment-4647852428) — have now run, so the head-to-head is no longer owed; it's answered.

**Verdict (gsm8k, ~1.5–1.7B student): pure RL beats OPD on accuracy *and* on compute-to-accuracy.**

| | accuracy (pass@8) | speed | converges in |
|---|---|---|---|
| **RL** — combo_acc(_stab), lr1e-5+n8+gen1024 | **~0.95–0.97** (≈task ceiling) | ~24–50 s/step | ~80–380 steps |
| **RL** — `base_q3`, **matched Qwen3-1.7B**, lr1e-6 | **0.94 peak** / 0.81 final | ~34 s/step | ~260 steps |
| **OPD** — base / topk16 (Qwen3-1.7B ← 32B) | ~0.82–0.83 (top3) | 836 → **387** s/step | ~16 steps |

On the **same student (Qwen3-1.7B), same task**, RL reaches **~0.94+** vs OPD's **~0.82**, while running **~10–20× cheaper per step** (≈19–50 s vs 387–836 s) — RL does ~40–70× more steps/hr. So both the accuracy ceiling and the pass@8-per-GPU-hour axis go to RL here.

**Why OPD loses the ceiling:** OPD distills toward the **Qwen3-32B teacher's distribution**, so its ceiling is the teacher — and 16 steps of distillation tops out at ~0.82–0.83. Pure RL is not teacher-bounded: gsm8k is small and **solvable from env reward**, so the policy climbs to the task ceiling (~1.0) on its own. A strong teacher doesn't help once the student can just solve the task. (Confirmed structurally by the OPD throughput grid: the **8B teacher fails the guard (0.578)** — a weaker teacher *lowers* the ceiling; teacher-size floor is >8B.)

**Mechanistic findings that fell out:**
- **GRPO lr knee = 1e-5**, two orders above OPD's distillation knee (3e-5). lr is the dominant lever in both, but the loss geometry differs.
- RL's near-ceiling result needs the **lr1e-5 × gen1024 combo** (neither alone clears 0.79) and an **entropy bonus** to avoid the collapse-to-0.04 that the bare lr1e-5 run shows. combo_acc_stab = ~0.95–0.98 *without* collapse.
- OPD is **93% teacher-forward-bound**; the only speed lever that paid is **top_k** (topk16 = 2.2× faster, lossless).

**Caveats — where this verdict does and doesn't hold:**
1. **Regime-specific.** gsm8k is small and saturable. The earlier MATH model-size sweep showed RL accuracy is *far* from ceiling at small sizes on harder math — on tasks the student **can't** solve from env reward alone, the 32B teacher signal (OPD) could still matter. This result is "small model, short-CoT, solvable task."
2. **Metric.** OPD pass@8 is a top-3-checkpoint mean; RL is last/peak. The ~0.94 vs ~0.82 gap dwarfs that difference, but they're not an identical estimator.
3. **OPD's biggest cost lever was never run.** Disaggregated teacher serving (teacher off the training GPUs) is deferred in the throughput grid — it would lower OPD's per-step cost, but it must close a ~10–20× gap to change the ranking, and it does nothing for the accuracy ceiling.

**Net:** for non-agentic gsm8k reasoning on Leonardo at this scale, **learning from env reward beats distilling a 32B teacher**, at lower compute. The open question OPD could still win is the harder-task / can't-solve-from-reward regime — that's the comparison worth running next, not another gsm8k pass.

comments.author: penfever
comments.body:
🤖 *(posted by an agent on behalf of @penfever)*

> **Update 2026-06-08 — both grids below have been EXECUTED.** Results: https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/6218#issuecomment-4647852428 · verdict: https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/6218#issuecomment-4643447025

## Next grids — the cross-designs (RL accuracy + OPD throughput)

The first two grids covered complementary corners: **RL** was a *throughput* sweep (sec/step, eff tok/s; reward unconverged at 25 steps, pass@8 never measured) and **OPD** was an *accuracy* sweep (pass@8 to ~0.75, but its speed cells ran at lr=1e-5 where nothing learned). To close the box — and to set up a clean controlled RL-vs-OPD head-to-head — here are the two complementary grids. Both run **to a real pass@8 readout** so the numbers are directly comparable across methods.

---

### Grid A — RL accuracy grid (gsm8k GRPO, Qwen2.5-1.5B, 1×4 A100-64GB)

**Goal:** the GRPO config that maximizes **gsm8k pass@8**, run **to a plateau** (not a 25-step probe). Metric = pass@8 (same eval harness as OPD) + **pass@8 per GPU-hour**; entropy/grad_norm as stability guard.

**Base = the throughput winner `combo_C`** (tbs128 · n8 · gmu0.85 · enforce_eager=false · micro16), 12,882 eff tok/s @ 20.7 s/step → ~175 steps/hr, so a to-convergence run fits an 8h wall easily. Raise `epochs` so wide-tbs cells don't exhaust the 7,473-row set before plateau.

**20 cells, 2 batches:**
- **Batch 1 — primary convergence levers (lr × group × CoT):** `base_long`, lr ∈ {3e-7, 1e-6, 3e-6, 1e-5, 3e-5} (re-find the GRPO knee — OPD's was 3e-5), n_samples ∈ {4, 16}, max_gen_len ∈ {1024, 2048}.
- **Batch 2 — stabilization + exploration + combos:** ref-KL {0.001, 0.01}, temperature {0.7, 1.2}, DAPO clip 0.28, entropy bonus, reward shaping (format/partial-credit), **`base_q3` = re-validate on Qwen3-1.7B** (OPD's student, for the head-to-head), then `combo_acc` (lr×n×gen winners) + `combo_acc_stab`.

> **Model-match note:** this grid inherits Qwen2.5-1.5B from the throughput base. For the apples-to-apples #6218 comparison the student should be **Qwen3-1.7B**; `base_q3` measures the rebase cost — decide before Batch 2.

Full plan (gist): https://gist.github.com/penfever/84faeb599d551625a93baaf7e2e99374

---

### Grid B — OPD throughput grid (Qwen3-32B teacher → Qwen3-1.7B student, gsm8k, 2×4 A100-64GB)

**Goal:** maximize OPD **throughput** (sec/step, steps/hr, **pass@8 per GPU-hour**) **while holding the converged accuracy** — re-optimize speed *around the accuracy optimum*, with **pass@8 ~0.75 as a HARD GUARD on every cell** (a cell that speeds up but drops pass@8 below ~0.70 is a *failed* speed cell).

**Base = the accuracy winner `combo_opt`** (lr3e-5 · top_k64 · n8 · gen1024 · teacher TP2 · colocated): pass@8 ~0.75–0.78, **832 s/step**. The bottleneck is known: OPD is **90–97% teacher-score-bound**, so throughput = cutting teacher-score cost without dropping pass@8. (The RL grid's gen/train levers are irrelevant here — student gen/train is <10% of the step.)

**20 cells, 2 batches:**
- **Batch 1 — teacher-serving + teacher-cost levers:** `base`, **`disagg`** (teacher on dedicated GPUs — biggest untapped lever, removes teacher↔student contention) + `disagg_mn`, teacher TP4, teacher FP8, teacher AWQ, **teacher size 14B / 8B** (the OPD-specific accuracy-vs-teacher-cost frontier), top_k ∈ {16, 32, 128} **re-validated @ lr3e-5** (the [OPD grid above](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/6218#issuecomment-4643446059) found these flat — but at lr1e-5 where nothing learned).
- **Batch 2 — scored-token + efficiency + combos:** gen512, n4, sequence-packing / chunked teacher scoring, student gmu0.85, then `combo_fast` (disagg+fp8+topk32), `combo_cheap_teacher` (14b+topk32+n4), `combo_fast_mn`, `combo_balanced` (best pass@8-per-GPU-hour corner).

**Headline metric: pass@8 per GPU-hour** (computed in GPU-hours — disaggregation and smaller teachers change the denominator). The key deliverable is the **teacher-size↔pass@8 frontier**: how small a teacher still distills gsm8k to ~0.75.

Full plan (gist): https://gist.github.com/penfever/bcbe186b1638ba36676ecce0d702d05e

---

Together these produce, for both methods, **pass@8 + pass@8-per-GPU-hour at a converged operating point** on the same eval harness — exactly the controlled comparison recommended in the analysis above. `base_q3` (Grid A) + the existing OPD Qwen3-1.7B student make the head-to-head model-matched.

| cell | knob | sec/step | steps/hr | KL Δ | pass@8 | guard | notes |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|---|:--:|---|
| gen512 | max_gen=512 | 471 | 7.64 | — | 0.188 last / 0.38 | ❌ **FAIL** | 512 truncates gsm8k CoT |

issues.author: dlwh
issues.body:
🤖
## Description
Follow-up to #6139 and related to #5328.

The current Grug ring EP path materializes global token/output buffers per rank. It all-gathers `x`, `selected_experts`, and `combine_weights`, gathers local expert assignments from `x_global`, then scatters into `out_global` before `psum_scatter` (`lib/levanter/src/levanter/grug/_moe/ep_ring.py:38`, `lib/levanter/src/levanter/grug/_moe/ep_ring.py:91`, `lib/levanter/src/levanter/grug/_moe/ep_ring.py:110`). For small d2560/top-4 shapes this plumbing is a large fixed cost relative to expert math.

Add an assigned-token EP path that moves only routed assignments and produces the layout expected by `ragged_dot`: `x_dispatch`, assignment weights, return metadata, and local expert `group_sizes`. This can be a simpler single-node all-to-all/ragged path or a DeepEP handoff that avoids the extra local repack in `_pack_deepep_local_assignments` and `segment_sum` collapse (`lib/levanter/src/levanter/grug/_moe/ep_deepep.py:50`, `lib/levanter/src/levanter/grug/_moe/ep_deepep.py:88`).

### Definition of Done
- No per-rank `x_global` or `out_global` activation buffer is required for the new path.
- Forward and backward match existing ring EP top-k combine semantics.
- Add a perf smoke test on the issue6044 d2560 shape comparing ring EP vs the new assigned-token path.
- Keep local GMM kernel work separate from this issue unless needed for the dispatch contract.

comments.author: claude[bot]
comments.body:
🤖 **Plan:**
- [x] Read issue and related code
- [x] Duplicate-work preflight (no open PR; #6139 is the parent transport-gap issue)
- [x] Decide scope: too large for an auto-PR (new EP backend, fwd+bwd parity, perf smoke); posting analysis instead
- [ ] Human review of proposed approach before implementation

# Research

Ring EP forces every shard to materialize `x_global` and `out_global` of shape `(tokens * ep_size, D)` even though each shard only consumes its local-expert slice. At d2560/top-4 the all-gather + scatter + `psum_scatter` plumbing dominates expert math. The two existing alternatives both pay extra cost: `ragged_all_to_all` uses a slow transport primitive on B200 (#6139 numbers), and the DeepEP path does a host repack (`_pack_deepep_local_assignments`) plus a `segment_sum` collapse before/after the GMM that an assignment-native contract would skip.

**Relevant code**
- [`ep_ring.py#L38-L40`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/levanter/src/levanter/grug/_moe/ep_ring.py#L38-L40) — three full all-gathers per call
- [`ep_ring.py#L91-L93`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/levanter/src/levanter/grug/_moe/ep_ring.py#L91-L93) — gather from `x_global`
- [`ep_ring.py#L110-L113`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/levanter/src/levanter/grug/_moe/ep_ring.py#L110-L113) — `out_global` scatter + `psum_scatter`
- [`ep_deepep.py#L43-L78`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/levanter/src/levanter/grug/_moe/ep_deepep.py#L43-L78) — extra local repack producing `x_dispatch` shape
- [`ep_deepep.py#L81-L97`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/levanter/src/levanter/grug/_moe/ep_deepep.py#L81-L97) — `segment_sum` collapse before combine transport

# Proposed Approach (design change, needs review)

Add a fourth EP backend `assigned_token` selected via the existing implementation knob at [`grug_moe.py#L208-L215`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/levanter/src/levanter/grug/grug_moe.py#L208-L215). New file `lib/levanter/src/levanter/grug/_moe/ep_assigned_token.py` exposes `_moe_mlp_ep_assigned_token_local(...)` with the same signature as the other three shard-local fns.

Dispatch contract: produce `(x_dispatch[TK_recv, D], assignment_weights[TK_recv], return_metadata, local_group_sizes[EL])` directly — the layout `ragged_dot` already consumes. No `x_global`, no `out_global`, no `segment_sum` collapse.

Sketch (shard-local, inside `shard_map("expert")`):

1. Per-shard expert-sorted permutation of routed assignments — reuse `_permute_by_global_expert` from `ep_common.py:44`. Each shard knows, for every global expert, how many of its own tokens land there.
2. Cross-shard sizing with one `all_gather` of the per-expert counts (small: `[num_experts]` int32, not `[tokens, D]` bf16). Derive `send_sizes` / `recv_sizes` for `ragged_all_to_all` of the routed-assignment payload — same shape calc as `ep_ragged_all_to_all.py:_shard_a2a_params` but built from per-edge counts so we never materialize `x_global`.
3. `ragged_all_to_all` of `(x_repeated_by_topk, combine_weight_repeated_by_topk)` into a receive buffer sized by `local_capacity = ceil(capacity_factor * assignments / ep_size)`. Capacity clipping reuses `_clip_receiver_group_sizes`.
4. Result is already grouped by local expert id → feed into `ragged_dot` directly (no `_pack_deepep_local_assignments` step).
5. Combine: multiply `out_dispatch` by `assignment_weights[:, None]` in place, then `ragged_all_to_all` with the transposed routing table back to the sender. On return, `_unpermute_from_global_expert` (already does the topk → token sum-combine) closes the loop.

Backward: the only custom-VJP-needing piece is the assignment permutation, which is already covered by `_sort_activations_custom` in `ep_common.py:17-31`. `ragged_all_to_all` has working autodiff on the existing path (`ep_ragged_all_to_all.py`), so reuse that.

Differences vs. `ragged_all_to_all` backend: that one keeps a per-shard `x_global`-equivalent (`sorted_x` with `assignments_per_shard` rows, then compacts via `keep_mask`). The proposed path sends only the post-capacity tail and removes the round-trip `_compact_by_keep_mask` / `_expand_from_keep_mask` pair.

Differences vs. `deepep`: skip `_pack_deepep_local_assignments` (the receive buffer is already grouped) and skip `_collapse_deepep_local_assignments` (weights applied on the dispatch side).

# Validation Plan

- Unit test in `lib/levanter/tests/grug/` parameterized over `(EL, ep_size, topk, capacity_factor)` that runs both `_moe_mlp_ep_ring_local` and the new fn under a CPU `shard_map` with a 4-device fake mesh and checks `allclose` on forward output and on the W13/W2 gradients. This is the DoD "fwd/bwd match ring EP" gate.
- Drop-counter parity: confirm `dropped_total` matches ring under low capacity.
- Perf smoke on d2560/top-4 from #6044 — separate `@pytest.mark.slow` benchmark that records ring vs assigned-token wall-time and prints the ratio. Not asserted; the artifact is what's reviewed.

# Open Questions

1. Is `jax.lax.ragged_all_to_all` differentiable on B200/TPU in the configurations Grug ships, or is the existing `ep_ragged_all_to_all` path relying on a workaround? If a custom VJP is needed, this becomes a 300+ LOC change rather than 150.
2. Should this share a file with `ep_ragged_all_to_all.py` (both use `ragged_all_to_all`) or stay separate for the perf-comparison story #6139 asks for?
3. Capacity model: ring uses `local_capacity = ceil(capacity_factor * tokens * topk / ep_size)`. The assigned-token path can either match that or use a tighter per-expert cap. Match ring exactly for the parity test, leave tuning for follow-up?

Estimated size: ~150-250 LOC new code + ~100 LOC test = above the 100-line auto-PR threshold, hence asking for review first.

comments.author: dlwh
comments.body:
🤖
# Research

Ring EP still pays for per-rank global activation buffers in dispatch/combine, so it is the right comparator but not the scalable endpoint. A first assigned-token reference path using `jax.lax.ragged_all_to_all` avoids `x_global`/`out_global`, but a 4-GPU B200 d2560/top-4 forward smoke measured it much slower than ring, so plain XLA collectives are unlikely to satisfy this issue. The next viable path is CUDA-backed assignment transport or DeepEP dispatch with CUDA-side assignment packing/collapse, not more XLA repacking.

**Relevant code**
- [`ep_ring.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/levanter/src/levanter/grug/_moe/ep_ring.py) - global-buffer comparator
- [`ep_deepep.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/levanter/src/levanter/grug/_moe/ep_deepep.py) - CUDA transport plus JAX repack/collapse
- [`transport_ffi.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/levanter/src/levanter/kernels/deepep/transport_ffi.py) - DeepEP JAX FFI/VJP surface
- [`deepep_transport_ffi.cu`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/levanter/src/levanter/kernels/deepep/csrc/deepep_transport_ffi.cu) - CUDA FFI implementation

# Proposed Fix

Add an explicit `assigned_token` EP backend and benchmark harness as the reference contract: `x_dispatch`, assignment weights, return metadata, and local `group_sizes`. Then move the hot path to CUDA by extending the DeepEP FFI side with local assignment pack/collapse kernels so Grug does not do `top_k`/`take`/`segment_sum` around DeepEP receive buffers. Keep ring as the perf/correctness comparator until the CUDA path beats it on the d2560/top-4 smoke.

issues.author: dlwh
issues.body:
<!-- experiment-tldr:start -->
## Summary

This probe compared upstream-shaped FlashAttention-4 THD/varlen attention against Marin's current Grug segmented FA4/CuTe path on B200 for the exact d5120 Grug causal attention shape. The measured THD compact `cu_seqlens` path was materially faster than the current segmented FA4/CuTe implementation across the tested packed layouts, but the usable prototype is still a torch/DLPack bridge rather than a JIT-safe JAX FFI. The recommended integration direction is fixed max-segment metadata plus a real THD/JAX FFI path, while avoiding the private JAX cuDNN packed-offset path until its exact-GQA numerics are validated.

### Helpful links
- https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/research/issue5815-fa4-thd-logbook-20260529/.agents/logbooks/issue5815-fa4-thd.md
- https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/6059
<!-- experiment-tldr:end -->

## Description

Issue5815 needs a narrow benchmark of upstream-shaped FlashAttention-4 THD/varlen attention against the current Grug dense BSHD segmented FA4/CuTe port on B200. The target shape is the exact d5120 Grug causal self-attention q/k/v layout: q `[B,S,Hq,D]`, k/v `[B,S,Hkv,D]`.

## Hypothesis or Goal

Determine whether reshaping BSHD to THD, building `cu_seqlens` from packed segment IDs or fixed segment metadata, and calling upstream FA4 CuTe varlen materially beats the current segmented FA4 path for fwd+bwd. Thresholds: `<=0.005s` promising, `0.005-0.010s` marginal, `>0.010s` not worth pursuing for issue5815.

### Links

* Stable research tag: https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/research/issue5815-fa4-thd-logbook-20260529
* Stable research logbook: https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/research/issue5815-fa4-thd-logbook-20260529/.agents/logbooks/issue5815-fa4-thd.md
* Stable probe script: https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/research/issue5815-fa4-thd-logbook-20260529/scratch/issue5815_attention_backend_probe.py
* Draft PR: https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/6059
* Code paths: `lib/levanter/src/levanter/grug/attention/_fa4_cute.py`, `lib/levanter/src/levanter/grug/attention/_core.py`, `lib/levanter/src/levanter/grug/attention/_fa4_thd.py`

## Results

Latest focused B200 probe for exact d5120, `S=4096,Hq=40,Hkv=8,D=128`, dynamic uneven segments:

| segs/row | B | dense upstream | current FA4/CuTe | THD fixed lengths | THD compact cu-lens |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 2 | 1 | 0.000681s | 0.001939s | 0.000892s | 0.000656s |
| 2 | 4 | 0.002399s | 0.006653s | 0.002391s | 0.002151s |
| 4 | 1 | 0.000680s | 0.001280s | 0.000790s | 0.000561s |
| 4 | 4 | 0.002343s | 0.004249s | 0.002028s | 0.001801s |

## Decision log

* 2026-05-29: The public upstream PyTorch varlen wrapper alone was not enough; internal upstream FA4 `_flash_attn_fwd/_flash_attn_bwd` is the relevant API for the THD/cu-lens core.
* 2026-05-29: Fixed max-segment metadata is a useful integration point. It is materially faster than current segmented FA4/CuTe and avoids scanning full `[B,S]` segment IDs in the attention hot path.
* 2026-05-29: Do not use the private JAX cuDNN packed-offset path for exact Grug GQA until its GQA numerics are validated.

## Negative results index

* Public `flash_attn_varlen_func` autograd was slower than the internal upstream fwd/bwd API.
* Private JAX cuDNN packed offsets were fast but failed numerics for exact `Hq=40,Hkv=8` GQA.
* Including full dynamic `segment_ids -> cu_seqlens` construction inside the timed helper can erase the THD kernel win on small cases.

## Current baseline

Shape `B in {1,4} S=4096 Hq=40 Hkv=8 D=128`, bf16, causal fwd+bwd, dynamic uneven contiguous segments. Latest focused medians are listed in Results.

**Relevant code**
- [`_fa4_cute.py#L130-L159`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/levanter/src/levanter/grug/attention/_fa4_cute.py#L130-L159) — current BSHD entry; consumes `AttentionMask.segment_ids`, computes per-token causal lower bounds, calls `fa4_cute_attention_forward`
- [`_fa4_cute_segmented_bwd.py#L44`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/levanter/src/levanter/grug/attention/_fa4_cute_segmented_bwd.py#L44) — "upstream varlen/THD cu_seqlens paths are intentionally disabled"
- [`_fa4_cute_kernels.py#L54-L58`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/levanter/src/levanter/grug/attention/_fa4_cute_kernels.py#L54-L58) — segmented kernel uses per-token bounds, not cu_seqlens
- [`_core.py#L21-L25`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/levanter/src/levanter/grug/attention/_core.py#L21-L25) — `GrugAttentionImplementation` literal lists only `reference`, `tpu_splash`, `gpu_fa4_cute`; no cuDNN or THD variant registered
- #5896 logbook — B200 FA4/CuTe baseline `(B=1,S=8192,Hq=32,Hkv=8,D=128,seg=256)` BF16: patched FA4 fwd+bwd `1.021 ms`, TE flash `1.229 ms`

# Proposed Approach

Design change — write before coding because the THD path does not exist.

Step 1: Add `fa4_thd_core` entry. New function in `_fa4_cute.py` that takes BSHD `q/k/v` plus `segment_ids`, reshapes BSHD → THD (`q: [B*S, Hq, D]`), and either (a) calls upstream `flash_attn.cute` varlen forward/backward directly with `cu_seqlens_q = jnp.arange(B+1, dtype=jnp.int32) * S` and `max_seqlen_q = S` — single-sequence-per-row, so the layout matches what the issue specifies — or (b) wires a thin JAX FFI wrapper around the CuTe varlen entry. Option (a) is preferred for the probe; (b) only if upstream lacks a JAX-callable handle.

Step 2: Add `jax_cudnn_core` reference. Wrap `jax.nn.dot_product_attention(..., implementation="cudnn")` with the same BSHD-in / BSHD-out signature so the three paths are directly comparable. jax cuDNN does not natively take packed segment_ids; for the probe use `is_causal=True` on the single-sequence-per-batch-row layout the issue defines.

Step 3: Write `scratch/issue5815_attention_backend_probe.py`. Driver that builds the d5120 Grug shape (issue does not pin `B/S/Hq/Hkv/D` — confirm with #5815; #5896 used `B=1, S=8192, Hq=32, Hkv=8, D=128`), runs each of `jax_cudnn_core`, `fa4_cute_core`, `fa4_thd_core` for fwd and fwd+bwd with a fixed `warmup=3, steps=10` loop, and prints steady-state ms plus value/grad max-abs vs a small-seq reference. Match the format used in the #5896 logbook so the result is appendable.

Step 4: Run on B200 (Slurm), apply the decision rule from the issue (`<=0.005s` promising / `0.005-0.010s` marginal / `>0.010s` skip) to fwd+bwd steady, and post the structured result back here.

Open questions to confirm before implementation:
- Target shape: take #5896 `(B=1,S=8192,Hq=32,Hkv=8,D=128)` or a different d5120 spec from #5815?
- Should `fa4_thd_core` call upstream `flash_attn.cute` varlen directly, or land a JAX FFI wrapper in `_fa4_cute_backend.py`?
- Who has B200 capacity to run this — should I prepare the probe script as a PR and hand off, or wait?

Estimated change size: ~150-300 LOC (probe + thd entry + cudnn entry + minimal test). Above the 100-LOC threshold, so awaiting confirmation before opening a PR.

- Change: Re-ran the probe with `B={1,2,4}` and `segment_len={4096,2048,1024}`. The cuDNN row now packs each contiguous segment into its own batch row before causal attention, so it matches multi-segment packed semantics instead of treating the full row as one sequence.

comments.author: dlwh
comments.body:
🤖 Update: dynamic unequal segment-length THD probe

- Change: Updated the probe to generate unequal contiguous segment lengths per row. The FA4 THD row uses compact THD `[total_tokens,H,D]` plus cumulative sequence lengths from segment starts. The cuDNN row uses padded segment rows plus sequence lengths because JAX cuDNN does not expose the same THD cumulative-length API.
- Result delta: For two uneven segments per row (`~[1365,2731]`), padded cuDNN errored on unsupported sequence length `2731`; THD beat current FA4/CuTe: `B=1` `0.001684s` vs `0.001970s`, `B=2` `0.002508s` vs `0.003547s`, `B=4` `0.004144s` vs `0.006702s`. For four uneven segments per row (`~[409,819,1228,1640]`), THD was slower at `B=1` but slightly faster by `B=2`/`B=4`: `B=4` THD `0.003757s` vs FA4/CuTe `0.004313s`.
- Confidence: exploratory; covers unequal contiguous segment lengths but not padded `-1` holes or non-contiguous repeated IDs.
- Links: `.agents/logbooks/issue5815-fa4-thd.md`, `scratch/issue5815_attention_backend_probe.py`.
- Next: Treat upstream THD/cu-seqlens as the dynamic packed candidate. Do not treat padded cuDNN as an equivalent replacement for arbitrary dynamic segment lengths.

comments.author: dlwh
comments.body:
🤖 Update: there is a lower-level JAX cuDNN packed-offset path that is not exposed through public `jax.nn.dot_product_attention`.

API used in the scratch probe:

`jax._src.cudnn.fused_attention_stablehlo.dot_product_attention(q, k, v, q_seqlen=..., kv_seqlen=..., q_offsets=..., kv_offsets=..., scale=1/sqrt(D), mask_type=MaskType.CAUSAL, qkv_layout="BTNH")`

For dynamic unequal contiguous segments, I pass inputs as `[B,S,H,D]`, `q_offsets/kv_offsets` as `[B,max_segments+1]`, and `q_seqlen/kv_seqlen` as `[B,max_segments]` with per-row segment lengths. This is closer to the packed/offset path we wanted than the public padded `jax.nn` sequence-length baseline.

B200 fwd+bwd medians for exact `S=4096 Hq=40 Hkv=8 D=128` dynamic Grug shape, one shape per Python process:

| segments per row | B | jax_cudnn_offsets_core |
|---:|---:|---:|
| 2 | 1 | 0.000708s |
| 2 | 2 | 0.001088s |
| 2 | 4 | 0.001878s |
| 4 | 1 | 0.000576s |
| 4 | 2 | 0.000880s |
| 4 | 4 | 0.001492s |

For comparison, the prior dynamic sweep had upstream FA4 THD at `0.001684/0.002508/0.004144s` for 2 segments at B=1/2/4 and `0.001591/0.002325/0.003757s` for 4 segments at B=1/2/4. Current local FA4/CuTe was slower than THD in the dynamic 2-segment case and roughly tied/lower only in the small 4-segment B=1 case.

Caveat: this is private `jax._src` API, not a stable public JAX surface. The offset path also showed process-level fragility when sweeping multiple offset shapes in one Python process: isolated one-shape processes completed, while a same-process shape sweep hit a CUDA illegal-address after a shape transition. That needs numerics and stability validation before any production use.

comments.author: dlwh
comments.body:
🤖 Correction on the private cuDNN offsets result: the fast `jax_cudnn_offsets_core` timings are not valid evidence for the exact Grug GQA shape yet.

I added a numerics check against `reference_attention` using the private offsets API with `MaskType.PADDING_CAUSAL` and start-offset encoding from the JAX docstring.

Results on a small dynamic segmented case, `S=1024 segments_per_row=4`:

| shape | output max abs | output mean abs | status |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| `Hq=40 Hkv=8` | 4.843750 | 0.166690 | invalid |
| `Hq=8 Hkv=8` | 0.015625 | 0.000476 | expected bf16 range |

The MHA control passing while the exact GQA shape fails points to a GQA + packed-offset limitation/bug in this private JAX/cuDNN path, not a simple segment-offset construction issue. So: yes, the private cuDNN path exists and is very fast, but I would not use it for issue5815 unless we can get/fix a validated GQA packed-offset API.

For now, upstream FA4 THD remains the valid dynamic-packed candidate from this probe; private cuDNN offsets are an interesting follow-up, not a drop-in replacement for the d5120 Grug shape.

| segs/row | B | dense upstream | current FA4/CuTe | THD fixed lengths | THD compact cu-lens |

issues.title: issue5815 FA4 THD attention probe

issues.author: WhenWen
issues.body:
<!-- experiment-tldr:start -->
## Summary

This experiment tested whether routed expert MuonH parameters in the May Grug MoE recipe should use a different learning-rate scale because each expert only sees a sparse subset of tokens. Gate 1 compared three normalizations: shrinking only routed expert LR by sqrt(sparsity), boosting the dense/non-expert MuonH LR, and a mid-ratio compromise. `boost-nonexpert` and `shrink-expert` both failed gate 1, while `mid-ratio` passed with modest effective speedups at d512 and d768, so gate 2 was launched for d1024 and d1280. The larger gate-2 run was still in recovery/monitoring in the latest issue updates, with most follow-up work focused on TPU preemptions, regional checkpoint restore, host RAM, and launcher fixes rather than a final gate-2 decision.

### Helpful links
- https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/5799#issuecomment-4474840407
- https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/5799#issuecomment-4477551329
- https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/5799#issuecomment-4480453273
<!-- experiment-tldr:end -->

## TL;DR

Test whether routed expert MuonH weights should use a smaller LR because each expert sees only a sparse fraction of tokens. Gate 1 compares two normalizations at d512 and d768 against the MoE effective-speedup gates.

## Original prompt

> I want to test the following idea on the per-expert learning rate, the per expert learning rate should be smaller as each expert see less token. My guess is that we should shrink the per-expert learning rate down by \sqrt{sparsity} (assuming sparsity is between [0,1]). On top of this idea, there are two potential candidate: we can either keep the learning rate on the remaining muonh parameters the same and decrease the per-expert learning rate; or keep the per-expert learning rate the same and increase the remaining learning rate. Let's try to do gate 1 for both and potentially do gate 2 if either pass gate1.

## Scope

Builds on #5763 (`may_arch + GN->MuonH + 1% warmup + no grad-clip`) and keeps that recipe fixed except for the MuonH LR split.

For may_arch, `num_experts_per_token=4` and `num_experts=256`, so `sparsity = 4 / 256 = 1/64` and `sqrt(sparsity) = 0.125`.

Gate-1 candidates:

| candidate | routed expert MuonH LR | remaining MuonH LR | Adam/AdamH groups |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| shrink-expert | 0.125x heuristic | 1.0x heuristic | unchanged |
| boost-nonexpert | 1.0x heuristic | 8.0x heuristic | unchanged |

Only routed expert MLP weights are in the `muonh_expert` bucket. Shared expert weights, attention matrices, and GatedNorm weights stay in the remaining MuonH bucket because they see dense traffic.

## Gate plan

Gate 1:
- d512 at 2.19e17 FLOPs
- d768 at 1.70e18 FLOPs

If either candidate shows effective speedup at both scales, run gate 2 for that candidate at:
- d1024 at 9.00e18 FLOPs
- d1280 at 2.83e19 FLOPs

## Links

- Branch: `moe_muonh_may_arch_per_expert_lr_gate1`
- Launcher: `experiments/grug/moe/muonh_may_arch_per_expert_lr_gate1.py`
- Research logbook: `.agents/logbooks/moe_per_expert_lr_sqrt_sparsity.md`

## Decision log

| Date | Decision | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| 2026-05-17 | Start with gate 1 only for both normalizations. | This isolates the LR normalization question before spending d1024/d1280 compute. |

## Negative results index

None yet.

## Current baseline

Use `experiments/grug/moe/README.md` compute-optimal baseline and `experiments/grug/moe/agent.md` effective-speedup gate definitions.

issues.author: yonromai
issues.body:
The TPU wheel refresh currently cold-installs the selected public vLLM and
tpu-inference wheel pair, then serves Qwen3-0.6B at tensor parallel size 8 on
`v6e-8`. This makes each refresh depend on an eight-chip slice. Qwen3-0.6B is
already the smallest model used by this test; the smaller resource shape is
tensor parallel size 4 on `v6e-4`.

[A previous fork refresh passed the served-Qwen3 test on `v6e-4`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/8616),
and [an earlier cold wheel consumer passed 22 of 22 requests on
`v6e-4`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/8323#issuecomment-5348879398).
The current public wheel pair has only been tested on `v6e-8`, so prove that
exact pair on `v6e-4` before changing the refresh procedure.

Keep the tpu-inference nightly at tensor parallel size 8 on its eight-chip TPU
alternatives. The nightly continues to cover the TP8 path while the refresh
test checks that Marin can install and use the exact release on a smaller
slice.

Done when:

- The exact wheel pair selected by a refresh is installed in a fresh `uvx`
  environment and served on `v6e-4` at tensor parallel size 4.
- The server becomes healthy, a real model request succeeds, and the receipt
  records the release, both wheel versions, Iris job and task IDs, and evidence
  that the job stopped and released the TPU.
- After that run passes, the refresh procedure uses `v6e-4` and tensor parallel
  size 4. It still runs only one TPU test and consumes the published wheels
  without rebuilding them.
- The fork policy diagram and test table name the new refresh hardware.
- The tpu-inference nightly keeps its TP8 coverage.

cc @rjpower

The vLLM overview can report collector status `healthy` when `prometheus_stage_failures` first appears positive inside the bounded scan or resets from a higher value to a positive value. The existing cumulative-counter delta drops both signals.

A predecessor-less positive sample should make status `incomplete` without becoming an exact in-window failure delta. A positive post-reset value should count as the definite post-reset contribution. Ordinary increases, zero or absent failures, cross-resource aggregation, and the ordered overview response should stay unchanged.

Original review: https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/8727#discussion_r3882211943
issues.title: [grafana] Collector health hides initial and reset failures

issues.author: weaverbot
issues.body:
The weekly fork-migration system from #8048 is in place: a refresh-fork skill and
per-fork descriptors (#8068, #8117), a weekly ferry coordinator (#8245) with Loom
federation (#8284), and automated re-pinning for the vLLM GPU wheel (#8292). The TPU
vLLM stack refreshed to tpu-inference v0.26.0 (#8207) on top of the externalized
stack (#8063), and the GPU wheel now discovers its `_C` extension by shape across the
CUDA 13 / stable-ABI boundary (#8250). This issue tracks the work that remains after
that rollout, and is the canonical fork-migration tracker going forward. It supersedes
#8048 and folds in the refresh trackers #8298, #7097, #7143, and #6480.

1. Promote the Harbor one-time catch-up. marin-community/harbor#73 re-ports the fork
   overlay onto current upstream and folds the standalone `harbor-config` package into
   `harbor.models`. It is mergeable with `marin-precommit`, `marin-style-sync`, and
   `tests` green. Two steps need an admin/reviewer: drop the retired `harbor-config`
   context from the fork `main` branch protection (it no longer reports, so it blocks
   the merge), then review and merge, and promote the caught-up tree to protected
   `main`. Done when fork `main` carries the caught-up overlay and its protection no
   longer requires `harbor-config`.

2. Bump the Marin Harbor pin. After harbor#73 lands, re-pin `config/external/harbor`
   to the landed `main` SHA, migrate the `harbor_config.*` imports in
   `lib/marin/src/marin/evaluation/harbor/trial_driver.py` to `harbor.models.*`, and
   keep the migration.toml [harbor] nuances. The aime-smoke e2e already passed
   end-to-end against the catch-up branch on qwen3-0.6b. Closes out the blocker path
   #8298.

3. Migrate MarinSkyRL as a managed Harbor consumer (#7920). The SkyRL fork depends on
   `harbor[analysis,datasets,daytona]` floating on `main` plus the standalone
   `harbor-config` wheel, so the harbor.models fold in harbor#73 breaks any SkyRL
   relock. Pin harbor to an explicit immutable ref, migrate off `harbor-config` to
   `harbor.models`, and give SkyRL a Marin-style update-external plus one terminal-bench
   e2e. Cadence stays decoupled and coordinated on breaking changes rather than weekly
   lockstep. Tracked under #7920.

4. Make the ferry's evalchemy leg observable. The weekly run produced no PR and filed
   no blocker for evalchemy. Confirm whether that is a legitimate no-op (the fork
   already matches upstream `main`) or a silent failure, and have the leg emit an
   explicit no-op summary either way.

5. Publish prebuilt TPU vLLM fork wheels (#7143). Cold TPU jobs still source-build the
   `vllm` and `tpu-inference` forks; a Marin-controlled index would let serve, eval,
   and RL install a pinned wheel. Standalone spec in #7143.

6. Resolve the Marin-owned pin audit (#6480). Decide whether Levanter can move to a
   Transformers 5 range and drop the tpu-inference Gemma4 guard, and keep the
   JAX/libtpu/torch/torchvision alignment documented against the fork stack. The
   descriptor records these as nuances; the decision is open. Spec in #6480.

issues.author: ClassicLarry
issues.body:
Add a Kimi Delta Attention (KDA) linear-attention path to the grug MoE model and interleave it ~3:1 with full softmax-attention layers, so long-context training/inference scales in compute and memory without the O(L^2) cost on every layer. The **primary success criterion is performant MFU on the KDA (linear-attention) layers** on GB200 (Blackwell SM100): a token-by-token recurrence is unusable, so the implementation uses the chunked-parallel delta-rule form (intra-chunk parallel matmuls + inter-chunk state recurrence), and must be SPMD-shardable across racks (no repeat of the FA4 device-0 failure mode).

## KDA algorithm
KDA (Kimi Linear, Moonshot) is the gated delta rule — DeltaNet with a data-dependent, **per-channel** forget gate. Per token, with recurrent state `S ∈ R^{d_k×d_v}`:

```
S_t = Diag(alpha_t) S_{t-1} + beta_t k_t (v_t - S_{t-1}^T k_t)^T
o_t = S_t^T q_t
```

- `alpha_t = exp(g_t) ∈ (0,1]^{d_k}` — per-channel decay (this fine-grained gate is what distinguishes KDA from scalar-gated Gated DeltaNet). `g_t = -exp(A_log)·softplus(low_rank(x)+dt_bias)`.
- `beta_t = sigmoid(...) ∈ (0,1)` — write strength.
- q,k are L2-normalized (eigenvalue stability of `I - beta k k^T`); q scaled by `1/sqrt(d_k)`.
- Output: RMSNorm + sigmoid gate + output projection.

Sources: Kimi Linear tech report (arXiv 2510.26692, KDA Eqs. 1–10), Gated Delta Networks (arXiv 2412.06464), Parallelizing Linear Transformers with the Delta Rule (arXiv 2406.06484), and `flash-linear-attention` (`fla/ops/kda/naive.py`, `fla/ops/gated_delta_rule/naive.py`).

## Chunked-parallel form (the MFU-critical piece)
Split length L into chunks of C=64. Per chunk, in fp32, with `b^r = cumsum(g)` per channel:
- Fold per-channel decay into q/k so all interactions are plain matmuls: `k_inflate = k·exp(b)`, `k_deflate = k·exp(-b)`, `q_inflate = q·exp(b)`.
- Delta-correction matrix `A[r,i] = -beta_r (k_inflate_r · k_deflate_i)` (strictly lower); invert unit-lower-triangular `(I - A)` by forward substitution → `T`.
- Pseudo-values `U = T (beta·V)`; decayed-key summary `k_cumdecay = T (beta·k·exp(b))`.
- Scan over chunks carrying `S`:
  `v_new = U - k_cumdecay·S`;
  `O = (q·exp(b))·S + Tril(q_inflate · k_deflate^T)·v_new`;
  `S <- Diag(exp(b^C)) S + (exp(b^C - b)·k)^T v_new`.

This is matmul-bound (C×C and C×d GEMMs) and pure JAX (no `custom_call`/callback), so XLA partitions it. It is a systematic per-channel broadening of the scalar `chunk_gated_delta_rule` already in-repo (`lib/levanter/src/levanter/layers/gated_deltanet.py`), which is validated against HF Qwen3-Next fwd+bwd (`lib/levanter/tests/test_gdn_kernels.py`) — we build/verify scalar-first, then broaden `g` to `[...,d_k]`.

## Hybrid layer schedule
Interleave ~3:1 KDA:full. Every `period`-th layer (default 4) plus the last is full causal softmax attention; the rest are KDA. This replaces the existing sliding/full schedule when the KDA hybrid is enabled; sliding window is dropped (KDA's decay + recurrent state provide local and global mixing). Kimi Linear uses head_dim 128, chunk 64, 3:1 ratio, NoPE on KDA layers.

## Integration plan
- `experiments/grug/moe/kda.py` (new): `recurrent_kda` (sequential reference) + `chunk_kda` (chunked-parallel), per-channel gate, batched over leading `(B,H)` dims.
- `experiments/grug/moe/model.py`:
  - `GrugModelConfig`: `kda_hybrid: bool`, `kda_full_attn_period: int`, `kda_chunk_size: int`.
  - `CausalSelfAttention`: add small decay/beta projections present on every layer (uniform pytree so the stacked `lax.scan` still works), used only on KDA layers; a KDA branch (no RoPE/XSA) that projects q/k/v, computes gates, runs `chunk_kda` under `shard_map`, applies output gate + `w_o`.
  - `Block.__call__`: `use_kda` flag selects softmax vs KDA.
  - Schedule extended to KDA-vs-full in both the unrolled and stacked-`lax.scan` paths (`cond` on an `is_kda` scan input, keeping the scan body uniform).
- `experiments/grug/moe/launch_cw_scale.py`: `SCALE_ATTN_IMPL=kda_hybrid` enables it; `SCALE_KDA_PERIOD` / `SCALE_KDA_CHUNK` tune it. These are config-build-time knobs, so no `dispatch.py` env-forwarding is needed.

## MFU plan
- Kernel: chunked-parallel pure-JAX (portable, XLA-partitionable, no callback), chunk 64. Consider a Pallas/Mosaic-GPU kernel only if the pure-JAX path leaves MFU on the table.
- Measure `throughput/mfu` from the grug trainer (wandb). Caveat: the analytic `lm_flops_per_token` counts full O(L^2) attention for every layer, so for KDA layers it over-counts and the reported hybrid MFU is a conservative lower bound; also compare tokens/sec/GPU of the hybrid vs the all-softmax baseline at matched config.
- Target: KDA-layer step time at or below the softmax layers it replaces at long seq (8k+), so the hybrid's tokens/sec/GPU exceeds the all-full-attention run.

## Sharding-safety requirement
The FA4 attention is bridged via `cutlass_call`→`jax.pure_callback`, which pins metadata to `{maximal device=0}` and breaks multi-rack SPMD (#7012, #6979). KDA must NOT reintroduce that: it is pure JAX and runs inside a `shard_map` over the batch axes (`replica_dcn,data,expert`) and head axis (`model`), with sequence/head_dim unsharded, so each device carries fully-local recurrent state with no collectives inside attention.

## Validation
- `chunk_kda` vs `recurrent_kda` (max-abs < 1e-4 fp32) across chunk sizes/shapes; scalar-limit cross-check vs levanter `recurrent_gated_delta_rule`.
- Tiny end-to-end grug fwd/bwd on CPU with `kda_hybrid=True`.
- Single-node GB200 MFU probe (shared cluster: check usage first, hold at most ~1 node/rack).

Part of #6711

comments.body:
I'd like to take this on. Before proposing anything, here's what I found exists since this issue was opened, and then what I'd build.

**What exists now (as of Aug 31)**

- **MaxText** has a pure-XLA chunked Gated Delta Rule used for Qwen3.5 training: `jax_chunk_gated_delta_rule` in `src/maxtext/models/qwen3.py` (intra-chunk WY-style precompute, inter-chunk `lax.scan`, fp32 state, chunk size configurable, wrapped in `jax.shard_map` in train mode). Apache-2.0. Limits relative to this issue: it's scalar-gated **GDN, not KDA**; **no `custom_vjp`** — gradients come from autodiff through the scan, which stores the fp32 state for every chunk (the same activation blowup that forced TP in #1884); **no segment resets** in training (segment IDs only feed conv-state extraction in inference, so packed documents leak state); tests are forward-only; no kernel.
- **sglang-jax** ships Pallas **KDA** kernels (`chunk_kda` prefill, `fused_recurrent_kda` decode) — TPU, inference-only, no backward (sgl-project/sglang-jax #948); its Qwen3.5 v1 GDN is a `lax.scan` (#1007). Google's Ironwood GDN kernels are likewise inference-side.
- **skyrl-tx** (SkyRL's JAX backend) merged Qwen3.5 dense and its maintainer publicly asked for chunkwise GDN *training* — so this op has a second customer given MarinSkyRL's lineage.
- On the PyTorch side, Qwen's **FlashQLA** (TileLang) reports 2–3× fwd / 2× bwd over FLA Triton on Hopper; that's the performance bar, not something callable from JAX.

As far as I can find, **no training-grade chunked KDA exists in JAX**, and the one training-grade chunked GDN (MaxText) lacks a memory-efficient backward, packed-sequence resets, and gradient tests. Pointers welcome if I've missed something.

**What I'd build, in landable pieces**

1. **PR-A:** fp32 naive KDA/GDN references ported from `fla/ops/kda/naive.py` and `fla/ops/gated_delta_rule/naive.py` (attributed), a real test suite (forward + gradient parity, packed-sequence equivalence, state round-trip, sharded==unsharded on an emulated mesh) replacing the permanently-skipped `test_gdn_kernels.py`, and an XLA chunked GDN ported from MaxText into grug conventions **with segment resets**.
2. **PR-B:** the KDA per-channel-gate variant (GDN kept as the tied-channel special case), plus a `custom_vjp` backward that checkpoints chunk-boundary states and recomputes intra-chunk terms — with measured peak memory vs. autodiff-through-scan.
3. **PR-C:** grug layer + config for a ~3:1 interleave (reusing the existing `short_conv` Pallas kernel for the causal conv), HF converter mapping, and a small matched-FLOPs ladder run vs. SWA+global with a long-context probe, written up as a W&B report + logbook.
4. **PR-D (stretch):** a Pallas-Triton kernel for the intra-chunk block with the inter-chunk scan left in XLA, behind a flag with the XLA fallback. Per the #3868 Mamba-3 conclusion I'd keep TPU XLA-first.

**Constraints I should be upfront about:** my hardware is L4/T4 plus TRC TPUs. I can validate correctness, sharding (CPU-emulated 8-device mesh), memory curves, and *relative* throughput (naive vs XLA-chunked vs Pallas) — but not the GB200 MFU criterion. Landing this would need a benchmark run on a rack from your side once PR-B/PR-D are green; I'll parameterize chunk size and checkpoint stride for that tuning.

**Questions**
1. Is a linear-attention path still on the roadmap for the next recipe, now that the hero run went SWA+global?
2. Is "validated on L4/TPU + team-run GB200 benchmark" an acceptable landing path?
3. GDN-first (PR-A) then KDA (PR-B) OK, or do you want KDA from the start?
4. Any preference on module location/naming under `levanter/grug/`?

I'll start PR-A regardless since the references and tests are useful either way.

issues.body:
Note: All text that follows was written by me with no AI-assistance :-)
# Overview

We would like to understand the influence of duplicated data on model performance and scaling laws. Prior work has identified that ‘duplicated data’ is hiding a lot of complexity: *how* the data is duplicated has a lot of impact on model scaling.

For instance, Hernandez et. al. find that the distribution of duplicated data influences how models scale. In particular, they find that for the same fraction of duplicated data,  repeating either a small sample of data many times or a big sample of data a few times has minimal effect on scaling, while a medium sample of data repeated a medium amount has stark negative effects. Kazdan et. al. find that semantic collisions are more harmful as the dataset and model size scale. They further note that in the training regime that contains many semantic collisions, scaling laws can break down unexpectedly (they provide an auxiliary term that mostly repairs them).

This motivates a rigorous study of how duplicated data influences model performance. We ask
* How does the mix of duplicated data affect how models scale?
* How does model scaling differ across different methods for deduplication, such as exact, fuzzy, and semantic?
* Are there cases in which duplicating quality data is better for training than other unique, but lower quality, data?
  * If so, how can we easily identify such data? For example, is the degree of duplication of some datapoint an indicator on how useful that datapoint is?

Studying these questions can motivate principled changes to Marin’s data standardization pipeline.

# Previous Experiments & Links

* [[Original Datakit Testbed Spec](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/c9dbd2709ad59fe2ee2f2833e5de19f474090802/docs/design/datakit_testbed.md)](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/c9dbd2709ad59fe2ee2f2833e5de19f474090802/docs/design/datakit_testbed.md)
* [[Initial Experiments](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/5200)](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/5200)
  * The experiments setup 3 model training runs
    * A baseline run, where data is sampled naturally with no deduplication applied
    * A fuzzy deduplication run, where data is sampled and then a dedupe pass is applied (this was slightly better than the baseline)
    * A run with 50% of the sampled data repeated (this was around the same performance as the baseline)

# Proposed Experiments

I have a few ideas

* Since the run with 50% duplicated data (equivalently, the run with 50% unique data) did not perform worse, we should push until we find how much unique data we need. We launch runs that use 25% unique data, 10% unique data, and 5% unique data and measure how performance is lost
  * Hypothesis: We’ll see a sort of power law where models get exponentially worse
  * We should properly regularize to make it fair, following from prior work by Kim et. al.
* Produce a scaling law curve for each of the 3 existing runs
  * Hypothesis: the curvature of the curves will be different, which might imply sensitivity to duplication
* There has been discussion on data that is superficially duplicate (e.g., templated data). What if the degree of duplication is a useful proxy for data quality? We can identify the top-N most duplicated data points in the testbed and remove them completely (not even leaving a unique version of it), ablating with the fuzzy dedup and baseline runs.
  * Hypothesis: highly repeated data (as calculated by the fuzzy dedup strategy) is actually not very useful

Other ideas include following up on the work on KRR and DSP predictions, investigating the robustness of simulated epoching scaling patterns when extrapolated to the full training run, or other connections to data mix.

# References

* Scale Dependent Data Duplication: Kazdan, J., Levi, N., Schaeffer, R., Chudnovsky, J., Puri, A., He, B., Donmez, M., Koyejo, S., & Donoho, D. (2026). Scale Dependent Data Duplication. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.06603
* Pre-training under infinite compute: Kim, K., Kotha, S., Liang, P., & Hashimoto, T. (2025). Pre-training under infinite compute. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.14786
* Scaling Data-Constrained Language Models: Muennighoff, N., Rush, A. M., Barak, B., Le Scao, T., Piktus, A., Tazi, N., Pyysalo, S., Wolf, T., & Raffel, C. (2023). Scaling Data-Constrained Language Models. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.16264
* Larger Datasets Can Be Repeated More: Yan, T., et al. (2025). Larger Datasets Can Be Repeated More: A Theoretical Analysis of Multi-Epoch Scaling in Linear Regression. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.13421
* Scaling Laws and Interpretability of Learning from Repeated Data: Hernandez, D., et al. (2022). Scaling Laws and Interpretability of Learning from Repeated Data. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2205.10487

issues.author: penfever
issues.body:
Marin cannot selectively resume a Harbor evaluation from its remote trial output. The adapter restores `harbor_trials/*/result.json` into the deterministic job directory, but it does not restore or seed Harbor's job-level `config.json`. Harbor returns from its existing-job scan when that file is absent, so `Job.create` treats the invocation as a fresh job. The isolated driver also exposes only `run`, so Marin cannot request Harbor's unscored-trial pruning behavior.

This blocks recovery from exhausted infrastructure failures without risking duplicate model trials. One affected run has 300 durable results: 297 have `verifier_result`, while three have `verifier_result=None` after `InternalServerError: Error code: 504 - {'error': 'upstream timeout after 120s'}`. A safe resume must retain the 297 scored trials and run only the three unscored trials.

Reproduce:
1. Run a Marin Harbor evaluation with remote output until it writes a mix of scored results and exhausted infrastructure failures.
2. Submit the same deterministic Harbor job and output path again.
3. Observe that [`_restore_completed_trials`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/2f49a34509fa414a770286cf28a2e09da7ac739b/lib/marin/src/marin/evaluation/harbor/runner.py#L110-L126) restores only trial directories and [`_run`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/2f49a34509fa414a770286cf28a2e09da7ac739b/lib/marin/src/marin/evaluation/harbor/trial_driver.py#L365-L367) calls `Job.create` without job-level resume metadata or a selective retry mode.
4. Harbor plans the full job instead of recognizing the restored scored trials; retaining every restored directory instead leaves exhausted unscored failures terminal.

Expected: the Marin-Harbor seam preserves every trial with `verifier_result is not None`, including reward zero, and schedules only missing, unreadable, or `verifier_result=None` trials. A regression test should round-trip a partial remote job and assert that scored trials are retained while only unscored trials are queued.

comments.author: penfever
comments.body: 🤖 Incident follow-up: Kueue preempted four batch inference children while their Harbor parents remained active. Iris correctly rescheduled the endpoints, but Harbor continued dispatching and exhausted 9, 9, and 4 trials in three affected runs before service recovered. The evidence and recovery sequence are recorded in [Echo incident #71](https://echo.oa.dev/wiki/71). This adds a second requirement alongside selective resume: endpoint-unavailable attempts should not consume per-trial retry budgets while a managed inference child is recovering.

🤖 Partially resolved on the Harbor side; the Marin seam lands in #7837.

Harbor (merged):
- marin-community/harbor#61 — preserve HF-dataset trials across rematerialization during resume (filed as part of this issue).
- marin-community/harbor#67 — classify incompatible preserved trials with structured exception data so an operator can tell extra attempts, removed tasks, and semantic changes apart.
- marin-community/harbor#53 — stop treating Daytona cache kwargs (auto_snapshot et al.) as resume identity, so toggling them no longer discards preserved trials.

Marin (the selective scored-retain / unscored-retry this issue's Expected section asks for) is in #7837: _prepare_resumed_job seeds the job-level config.json Harbor's resume scan requires and prunes unscored (verifier_result=None) trials, while _migrate_legacy_scored_trials imports only scored trials from the legacy harbor_trials/ root; the regression test test_resume_preparation_keeps_scored_trials_and_prunes_unscored covers the 297-scored / 3-unscored case. #7837 is still open.

issues.body:
The TPU canary ferry (Grug MoE smoke test) crashes at compile time on the first `train_step`. On this run the crash was deterministic across all 4 task attempts, so `max_task_failures` was exceeded and the job failed.

The expert grouped-matmul fails to lower on TPU v6e: the megablox GMM `pallas_call` builds an output `BlockSpec((512, 32))` for an output array of shape `(524288, 128)`. Pallas requires the last block dim to be divisible by 128 or equal to the array dim; 32 is neither.

```
ValueError: The Pallas TPU lowering currently requires that the last two
dimensions of your block shape are divisible by 8 and 128 respectively, or be
equal to the respective dimensions of the overall array. Block spec for outputs
in pallas_call kernel at .../pallas/ops/tpu/megablox/gmm.py:393 has block shape
(Blocked(block_size=512), Blocked(block_size=32)), array shape (524288, 128)
```

Call path: `levanter/grug/_moe/scatter.py:48` (expert MLP projection), then `haliax.nn.ragged_dot._ragged_dot_megablox_impl` (`lib/haliax/src/haliax/nn/ragged_dot.py:93`), then `jax.experimental.pallas.ops.tpu.megablox.gmm`. The output n=128 equals the canary model intermediate_dim.

Reproduce:
1. Run the TPU canary ferry `python -m experiments.ferries.canary_ferry` on `v6e-4` (`CANARY_MODEL`: hidden_dim=32, intermediate_dim=128, num_experts=32, num_experts_per_token=2, num_layers=4).
2. The failure is intermittent across scheduled runs (history below); it reproduces when the megablox GMM lowers fresh instead of loading from the shared JAX compilation cache.

Expected: the megablox GMM lowers with a valid output block (last dim divisible by 128, or equal to n) and the canary trains to the regression gate.

<details><summary>Root-cause status (unresolved discrepancy)</summary>

The observed tn=32 does not match the checked-out tiling logic. `_megablox_tile_size()` at HEAD returns an n-tile of 1024, so `_ragged_dot_megablox_impl` passes `tiling[2] = min(n=128, 1024) = 128`, which would produce a valid `(512, 128)` output block. Static reading of the current code does not explain how tn=32 was emitted. This gap is the crux and needs a kernel owner.

Signals pointing away from a fresh code regression on the commit for this run:
- The prior scheduled canary (2026-08-27 06:30 UTC, `f8972ac`) succeeded. The three commits since (PR 8721 external eval/RL runtimes, PR 8717 echo dashboard, PR 8710 IAM grant) touch no JAX, haliax, levanter, or grug code.
- `ragged_dot.py` last changed 2026-08-25 (PR 8610), before two successful runs.
- Canary history alternates pass/fail (Aug 26 pass, Aug 27 06:30 pass, 03:42 and 17:21 fail).

The failing attempt logged a compilation-cache read failure immediately before the crash:
```
UserWarning: Error reading persistent compilation cache entry for
jit__create_lm_example: RuntimeError: Session is closed
```
Shared cache: `gs://marin-eu-west4/tmp/ttl=30d/compilation-cache`. Leading hypothesis: a latent megablox tiling incompatibility for these shapes, normally masked by compilation-cache hits and exposed when the cache read fails and the kernel lowers cold. Not confirmed.
</details>

comments.body:
🤖 Research

The invalid Megablox grouped-matmul output block is produced in the left-hand-side gradient path. Haliax passes the concrete forward tile `(512, 128, 32)` into JAX Megablox's custom VJP; `grad_lhs` swaps the contraction and output dimensions, then reuses that tuple and produces output block `(512, 32)` for an array with 128 columns. The compilation-cache read failures coincided with cold lowering in the reported runs, but the reused forward tile causes the compiler error.

Proposed Fix

[PR #8719](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/8719) already changes Haliax to pass a callable tiling policy, so each forward or backward grouped matmul computes a tile for its own shape; the left-hand-side gradient selects `(512, 32, 128)`. No duplicate implementation was opened. The PR has green GitHub checks, exact-shape v6e-4 parity with XLA for loss, forward output, and both gradients (maximum absolute difference `0.0`), and a [canary run](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/actions/runs/33046136662) that displayed 238/238 while its validator recorded 237 completed steps and final finite loss `5.7976`. It is open and needs review and merge. The incident record is at [Echo](https://echo.oa.dev/wiki/264).

issues.author: jamt9000
issues.body:
As of #7820 the expert FF parameters are stored in a big `[n_layers, n_experts, d_in, d_out]` tensor, eg `[48, 384, 3072, 3072]`, with the specialised [`_newtonschulz_4d_distributed`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/5da0277745729230801f91e0181406f291099f9d/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/grugmuon_hero.py#L211) computing Newton Schulz on the last two dimensions.

However, in the optimizer, the axes used to compute the norm will end up as `(1,2,3)`, which includes the expert dimension.

https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/5da0277745729230801f91e0181406f291099f9d/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/optimizer.py#L76

This seems to be unintentional, since that optimizer code was originally to handle 3D `[n_experts, d_in, d_out]` shapes in #6153.

The implication is that an updated matrix parameter **M**<sub>t+1</sub> will **no longer be constrained to its original hypersphere** of norm ||**M**<sub>t</sub>||<sub>F</sub> as described in MuonH originally. Instead the combined cat([**M**<sub>t+1</sub><sup>expert1</sup>, **M**<sub>t+1</sub><sup>expert2</sup>, ...]) will be constrained to norm ||cat([**M**<sub>t</sub><sup>expert1</sup>, **M**<sub>t</sub><sup>expert2</sup>, ...])||<sub>F</sub> allowing individual matrices to grow or shrink within that constraint. Although not necessarily a terrible thing to do (experiments in https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/5253 tried both for AdamH).

comments.author: ClassicLarry

Though NS is ran per expert, so this blurs the representation.

> I think its conceptually reasonable to think of all routed experts as a single matrix that is sparsely activated for each token. Though NS is ran per expert, so this blurs the representation.

I was having similar thoughts, it's interesting how Muon basically treats any matrix-shaped thing as a matrix when some of that is down to data layout decisions on whether to pack multiple logical matrices into one. Say with W_q in attention it could be represented as n_heads separate matrices, which wouldn't affect the forward but would cause different optimiser dynamics of doing Newton-Schulz and hyperball projection on each head matrix separately. Likely it doesn't make a huge difference either way. But as you say different dims for NS and norm is probably a bit weird. 

Edit: turns out for the attention matrix split there's some research into it [When and Why Grouping Attention Heads Accelerates Muon Optimization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.08933) so could be a similar effect with expert grouping
