issues.author: rjpower
issues.body:
The Marin codebase needs to maintain a high level of quality to preserve development velocity. As agents have increased the rate of code production, the burden of doing code reviews has increased as well. While we don't demand code review for every PR, we still rely on it for important new code additions and to ensure code fits our guidelines.

One area we're particularly concerned about is slop. Agents produce "slop" in a way and scope well beyond a normal human coder: documentation or comments written in a bizarre style, oddly baroque abstractions, or repetitive coding practices. As a reviewer, it's frustrating and tiring to have to comment on slop code.

We have an initial set of agentic linting rules tied into our commit process that were mostly created from scratch. This proposes a weekly process to automatically refine and improve these rules based on observed reviewer feedback: rules which have never triggered are removed, and new rules introduced to capture common patterns, measured automatically and rolled out against a benchmarking set to ensure we don't regress.

## Current status

Our review process tracks findings by rule and user. Currently 3,672 findings across 61 distinct rules; the top 12 rules account for ~62% of findings, with the remaining 49 rules accounting for 37.4% (1,373).

Top rules by finding count:

| Rule | Findings | Share |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| ml-tuple-return-shape | 285 | 7.8% |
| ml-duplicate-logic-block | 277 | 7.5% |
| ml-magic-constant | 245 | 6.7% |
| ml-overloaded-function | 245 | 6.7% |
| ml-impl-narration-docstring | 244 | 6.6% |
| ml-slop-test | 243 | 6.6% |
| ml-unused-param | 216 | 5.9% |
| ml-echo-across-files | 154 | 4.2% |
| ml-module-globals | 108 | 2.9% |
| ml-env-var-vs-param | 97 | 2.6% |
| ml-duplicate-constant | 93 | 2.5% |
| ml-misleading-name | 92 | 2.5% |
| Remaining 49 rules | 1,373 | 37.4% |

A spot review shows these reviews are almost always acted on by the development agent, implying even the ad-hoc reviews have saved thousands of user interactions. Despite this, we still regularly post PRs full of agentic slop, with plenty of room for improvement.

## Proposal

Two levers:

- **Better enforcement:** auto-reject PRs that don't have the `agentic-review` tag assigned to them. This should force agents that forgot the agentic review process to trigger review.
- **Better quality:** every human comment on a PR is something that *could* have been caught during agentic PR review. Analyze these weekly and identify the comment types that recur most frequently and are easiest to resolve.

## Approach

- Move statistics out of WandB and into Finelog via a bulk import & CLI adjustments
- Add a Grafana dashboard for monitoring & alerting rules as appropriate
- Set up a weekly GitHub action which:
  - **Fetch:** all PRs with comments in the last week
  - **Triage:** which comments are actionable for linting
  - **Review:** which rules haven't fired for > 1 month
  - **Adopt:** new rules which would have captured the failure patterns

## Success criteria

- A live dashboard on Grafana showing agentic code review feedback statistics, including triggers, feedback quality metrics, timing (too slow a feedback loop and users get impatient), and any issues we run into
- Weekly report sent to Slack with our PR statistics
- A codified, tentatively weekly, auto-improvement process for our agentic linting patterns

Long-term success metric: *does the number of PR comments that could have been caught by agentic linting go down over time?* This is not a hard metric — it will fluctuate as coding standards change and as agents get more powerful — but in general we want to see it go down.

## Rollout

Bulk upload of all agentic lint data into Finelog with the initial rollout, then set up GitHub actions for the maintenance loop.

## Expected timeframe

~1 day of work, which can be overlapped with other ongoing projects.

## Alternatives considered

**Do nothing.** Rejected: this is a low-effort way to reduce human reviewer load.

**Adopt some external service.** Rejected: lack of a self-reinforcement cycle, and an initial survey found no external service provided significantly higher value.

comments.author: rjpower
comments.body:
🤖 Research

The Finelog migration is live, but [`review.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/1ce93369edc85d24e9b38bbac3f7e560e8548815/infra/codehealth/review.py) has no scheduled caller and the latest classified human-review rows are from June 24. The current [PR review workflow](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/1ce93369edc85d24e9b38bbac3f7e560e8548815/.github/workflows/ops-claude-review.yaml) launches two Claude jobs, while the [commit workflow](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/1ce93369edc85d24e9b38bbac3f7e560e8548815/.agents/skills/commit/SKILL.md) leaves no durable proof that its local agentic lint pass ran. I found no open PR overlapping #8738.

Proposed Fix

The first PR will replace the Claude jobs with a secretless, workload-federated Weaver review; require the `agentic-lint` label that the commit workflow adds after its local review; schedule aggregation and reporting; and preserve inline diff context when classifying review comments. It will include behavior tests and update the [code-health operator documentation](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/1ce93369edc85d24e9b38bbac3f7e560e8548815/infra/codehealth/README.md). The benchmark corpus, rule refinement engine, and the one-month no-exposure removal policy will follow in a second PR.

comments.author: rjpower
comments.body:
🤖 Research

The current PR proves complete GitHub review collection, but it rebuilds an archive for each run and hard-codes matching, analysis, and report rendering. The survey needed repeated thread inspection and rule probing, so those judgments belong to an exploratory agent. The shared `marin-metadata` PostgreSQL service can persist the 30-day review window and incremental cursors directly; no GCS corpus archive is required.

Proposed Fix

Rewrite #8747 around PostgreSQL-backed review and lint activity, structured YAML lint rules, and bounded agent tools for listing PRs/comments, fetching comment context, and probing a selected rule with a caller-selected model and effort. The scheduled agent will edit catalog YAML, open a normal templated PR, author its own Loom report and charts, and send the report link to `marin-eng`; fixed feedback matching and report-rendering code will be removed.

spillover_issues.author: yonromai
spillover_issues.body:
The infra nightly matrix reduces every observed run to healthy or unhealthy. Although the GitHub bridge reads the run's `queued`, `in_progress`, or `completed` status, `/github/nightlies` does not return it. A queued or in-progress run is therefore rendered as a red failure until it completes.

The header compounds this by reporting only `healthy / due`, which groups running, failed, missing-run, and unavailable states together. The legend does not define running or unavailable, and `missing` does not tell a new viewer that GitHub created no run.

This was visible on August 31 when [Datakit tier 2](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/actions/runs/33405458686) was in progress but appeared failed, while overdue schedules with no GitHub run appeared in the separate dark-red missing state.

Expected behavior:

- Show queued and in-progress runs as blue `Running`, with elapsed time.
- Show an overdue schedule with no observed GitHub run as `No run`.
- Keep completed success green, completed or quality-gate failure red, slow success amber, datasource unavailable orange, and not-yet-due neutral.
- Pair every color with a distinct icon and plain label, and explain every state in the legend and tooltip.
- Replace the healthy ratio with categorical counts such as `3 passed · 1 running · 4 no run · 2 failed`.

Do not change cron schedules, grace periods, or nightly quality gates. This issue only makes the dashboard report its existing observations clearly.

cc @rjpower

spillover_issues.author: dlwh
spillover_issues.body:
## Description
Generalize the paged-attention execution config introduced in #6099 from `TpuPagedAttentionConfig` to a backend-neutral `PagedAttentionConfig` draccus choice family.

The current config combines backend selection with TPU-specific tuning fields. That is already awkward for `tpu-inference` versus JAX RPA, and it will get worse once a GPU implementation lands. Keep the policy passed through decode, but make the config type generic and dispatch by concrete choice type rather than a TPU-only enum.

Suggested choices: `auto`, `reference`, `tpu-inference`, `jax-rpa`, and later a GPU backend choice.

### Definition of Done
- `decode` and attention call sites accept `PagedAttentionConfig`, not `TpuPagedAttentionConfig`.
- TPU-specific tunables live only on TPU-specific choice dataclasses.
- `paged_attention_with_kv_update` dispatches by config choice type.
- Existing TPU paged-attention tests cover the renamed/generic config surface.

**Research**

The code this issue refers to lives only on the open draft [PR #6099](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/6099) (`codex/levanter-tpu-paged-attention`); nothing matching `TpuPagedAttentionConfig` / `paged_attention_with_kv_update` is on `main` yet. The current `TpuPagedAttentionConfig` mixes three concerns: backend selection (generic), dispatch policy (`allow_autotune`, `fail_on_reference_fallback` — generic), and backend-specific tunables (`tpu_inference_out_dtype`, `preserve_attention_output_dtype` for tpu-inference; `num_kv_pages_per_block`, `num_queries_per_block`, `vmem_limit_bytes` for JAX RPA). Dispatch is a string-enum if/elif chain in `_run_backend`, so adding a GPU backend later means widening every model signature and growing the enum/branch list.

Relevant code (PR #6099 branch):
- [`tpu_kernels.py#L22-L41`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/codex/levanter-tpu-paged-attention/lib/levanter/src/levanter/inference/tpu_kernels.py#L22-L41) — `TpuPagedAttentionBackend` enum + `TpuPagedAttentionConfig` dataclass.

- [`attention.py#L1777`, `#L1961`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/codex/levanter-tpu-paged-attention/lib/levanter/src/levanter/layers/attention.py#L1777) — call sites in `PagedKvCacheAttention.decode` variants.

- [`test_tpu_paged_attention_backends.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/codex/levanter-tpu-paged-attention/lib/levanter/tests/inference/test_tpu_paged_attention_backends.py), [`test_qwen3.py#L18`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/codex/levanter-tpu-paged-attention/lib/levanter/tests/test_qwen3.py#L18) — tests that construct the config.

**Proposed Approach (for review before implementing)**

1. New module `lib/levanter/src/levanter/inference/paged_attention_config.py`:
   - Abstract base `PagedAttentionConfig` registered with draccus as a choice family.
   - Generic policy fields on the base: `fail_on_reference_fallback: bool`, plus multi-backend ordering handled via a wrapper like `AutoPagedAttentionConfig(candidates=...)` rather than a magic `AUTO` enum value.
   - Concrete choices: `ReferencePagedAttentionConfig`, `JaxRpaPagedAttentionConfig` (holds `num_kv_pages_per_block`, `num_queries_per_block`, `vmem_limit_bytes`), `TpuInferencePagedAttentionConfig` (holds `out_dtype`, `preserve_attention_output_dtype`, `vmem_limit_bytes`), and later `GpuPagedAttentionConfig`.
   - Each choice exposes a `run(q, new_k, new_v, kv_cache, batch_info, *, sm_scale, soft_cap) -> tuple[NamedArray, KvPageCache]` method; `paged_attention_with_kv_update` becomes a thin entry point that walks the candidate list, catches `UnsupportedPagedAttentionBackend`, and emits a fallback warning. No `if/elif backend == ...` chain remains.

2. Rename the `tpu_paged_attention` parameter on `PagedKvCacheAttention.decode`, `LlamaDecoderLayer.decode`, `LlamaTransformer.decode`, `LlamaLMHeadModel.decode`, and the Apertus equivalents to `paged_attention: PagedAttentionConfig`. Default to `AutoPagedAttentionConfig()`.

3. Keep `TpuPagedAttentionShape` and platform/shape gating helpers, but move them into the TPU-specific choice classes (they call `tpu_paged_attention_supports_shape` internally). No backward-compat shim per AGENTS.md "NO BACKWARD COMPATIBILITY".

4. Update `test_tpu_paged_attention_backends.py` and `test_qwen3.py` to construct concrete choices (`JaxRpaPagedAttentionConfig()`, `TpuInferencePagedAttentionConfig()`, `ReferencePagedAttentionConfig()`) and parameterize on those directly instead of the string enum.

5. Estimated diff: ~400-600 lines across `tpu_kernels.py` (split into `paged_attention_config.py` + `tpu_pallas_backend.py`), `tpu_inference_adapter.py` (no signature change), `attention.py`, `llama.py`, `apertus.py`, two test files. Above the <100 LOC PR threshold, hence this design comment instead of a direct PR.

**Open questions for the issue author**

- Should the choice family base live in `levanter.inference` (next to backends) or in `levanter.layers.attention` (next to the call sites)?
- Is `AutoPagedAttentionConfig(candidates=[...])` the preferred way to express the current `AUTO` policy, or do you want a top-level `auto` choice that internally re-resolves to a platform-derived default each call?
- Confirm the `fail_on_reference_fallback` semantics belong on the base config rather than only on `ReferencePagedAttentionConfig` — keeping it on the base preserves today's "I picked tpu-inference and refuse to silently fall back to reference" behaviour.

Will wait for confirmation on #6099 merging and the questions above before opening a PR.

spillover_issues.author: dlwh
spillover_issues.body:
🤖
## Description
Add target-only PPL eval slices for low-level text and interpreter mechanics. The eval should cover exact token-to-character decomposition across every Marin tokenizer id that is representable in normal UTF-8 text, report byte-fallback/replacement-character ids that cannot round-trip through JSONL text, and include small circuit-style probes for character counts, indices, line lengths, indentation, arithmetic, and Python REPL surfaces.

### Definition of Done
- Generate eval-only JSONL records with `input`, `target`, and provenance metadata.
- Verify every representable non-special Marin tokenizer id included in vocab coverage appears in at least one rendered input as that token id.
- Emit a coverage summary for excluded ids that cannot be exposed as normal Unicode text.
- Register the bundle in the perplexity-gap registry for Marin 32B vs Qwen3 32B scoring.
- Add focused tests for tokenizer coverage verification, target-only rendering, metadata/tags, and local JSONL staging.
- Provide the dry-run/run command for the scoring job and record the output artifact paths when run.

comments.author: claude[bot]
comments.body:
🤖 **Plan:**
- [x] Read issue and check actionability
- [x] Duplicate-work preflight (open PRs/issues)
- [x] Survey existing eval-slice pattern and registry
- [x] Post Research + Proposed Approach for human review
- [ ] Await design confirmation before implementation (scope exceeds the 100-line PR threshold for agent-authored fixes)

# Research

Issue asks for a new target-only PPL bundle covering tokenizer/interpreter mechanics (char counts, indices, line lengths, indentation, arithmetic, Python REPL) plus a vocab-coverage invariant over the Marin tokenizer, and registration in the perplexity-gap registry against the existing \`marin_32b\` vs \`qwen3_32b\` pair. No existing slice covers this — the closest analogs are the identifier-encoding and delimiter-format families.

Definition of done is concrete, but two design choices need a human decision before code lands: (a) storage surface for the bundle, and (b) what \"every non-special token id appears\" means in practice given the ~100k Marin vocab.

**Relevant code**
- [\`experiments/evals/synthetic_identifier_encoding_ppl.py\`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/experiments/evals/synthetic_identifier_encoding_ppl.py) — template for slice family + JSONL writer + sample harness
- [\`experiments/evals/synthetic_delimiter_format_ppl.py#L385-L411\`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/experiments/evals/synthetic_delimiter_format_ppl.py#L385-L411) — alternative pattern using local \`StepSpec\` materialization (no HF push)
- [\`experiments/evals/perplexity_gap_registry.py#L113-L183\`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/experiments/evals/perplexity_gap_registry.py#L113-L183) — bundle factories, \`registered_perplexity_gap_bundles\`, and the \`marin_32b\` / \`qwen3_32b\` pair already exist
- [\`lib/marin/src/marin/evaluation/perplexity_gap.py#L116-L142\`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/marin/src/marin/evaluation/perplexity_gap.py#L116-L142) — \`supervised_text_dataset\` is the target-only entry point
- [\`experiments/exp_model_perplexity_gap_coverage_matrix.py\`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/experiments/exp_model_perplexity_gap_coverage_matrix.py) — dry-run / run command; new bundle is picked up automatically once registered

# Proposed Approach

New module \`experiments/evals/circuit_coverage_ppl.py\` modeled on \`synthetic_identifier_encoding_ppl.py\`:

1. \`CircuitCoverageFamily(StrEnum)\` with six task families: \`vocab_coverage\`, \`char_counts\`, \`char_indices\`, \`line_lengths\`, \`indentation\`, \`arithmetic\`, \`python_repl\`. One \`CircuitCoveragePplSlice\` per family with tags \`loss:target_only\`, \`epic:5005\`, \`issue:6103\`, \`source:generated_circuit_coverage_ppl_v1\`, seed/examples, family/task.
2. Deterministic row generator (RNG seeded per row, same \`seed + slice_offset + row_index\` pattern) producing \`{input, target, id, subset, task, seed, metadata}\` JSONL records. Each family is small and probe-style:
   - \`char_counts\`: \"How many 'x' in 'abxxcx'? Answer: \" → \`3\\n\`
   - \`char_indices\`: \"The 4th char of 'abcdef' is \" → \`d\\n\`
   - \`line_lengths\`: \"Line length of 'foo bar baz': \" → \`11\\n\`
   - \`indentation\`: snippets with 2/4/8-space and tab leading prefixes; predict the continuation indent
   - \`arithmetic\`: small base-10 add/sub/mul, target is digits-only continuation
   - \`python_repl\`: short \`>>> expr\\n\` interactions where target is the next \`>>> \` line or the result
   - \`vocab_coverage\`: see below
3. **Vocab-coverage invariant**: load \`marin-community/marin-tokenizer\` once, enumerate \`{id: token}\` excluding \`all_special_ids\` and any \`added_tokens_decoder\` entries marked special. For each non-special id, emit a row whose rendered \`input + target\` re-tokenizes to a sequence containing that id at least once. Cheapest construction: \`tokenizer.decode([id])\` round-tripped through a fixed framing prompt (e.g. \`\"Token: \" + decoded + \"\\n\"\`), then verified by re-encoding under \`add_special_tokens=False\`. Rows where the round-trip drops the id (mojibake / merge boundary issues) get a fallback construction that places the decoded fragment between two known-stable anchor strings until the id reappears; if no construction works after N attempts, raise (fail fast — invariant must be true by construction, not by chance).
4. Tests in new \`tests/evals/test_circuit_coverage_ppl.py\`:
   - Tokenizer coverage: load tokenizer, generate \`vocab_coverage\` slice, assert \`{id} ⊆ tokens(input+target for every row)\` covers \`vocab − special_ids\`. Real tokenizer, no mocks.
   - Target-only rendering: every row has non-empty \`input\` and \`target\`; both keys round-trip through \`supervised_text_dataset\` and produce a \`RawTextEvaluationDataset\` with \`input_key=\"input\"\`, \`target_key=\"target\"\`.
   - Metadata/tags: each slice's \`tags\` tuple contains the required tags; \`metadata\` carries \`family\` and probe-specific keys.
   - Local JSONL staging: \`write_circuit_coverage_jsonl_configs(tmp_path)\` produces one file per slice, each line valid JSON with the required schema.
5. Registry: add \`circuit_coverage_bundle()\` in \`experiments/evals/perplexity_gap_registry.py\` and append it to \`registered_perplexity_gap_bundles()\`. The existing \`PerplexityGapPair(\"marin_32b\", \"qwen3_32b\")\` then picks it up automatically.
6. Scoring command (no new entry point needed):
   \`uv run python experiments/exp_model_perplexity_gap_coverage_matrix.py --dry_run\` for dry-run, drop \`--dry_run\` for the real run. Artifact paths land under \`analysis/model_perplexity_scores/circuit_coverage/{marin_32b,qwen3_32b}\` and \`analysis/perplexity_gap/circuit_coverage/marin_32b-vs-qwen3_32b\`.

# Open questions for the issue author

1. **Storage surface**: HF-hosted (like \`marin-community/synth-identifier-encoding-ppl\`) or local-only via \`StepSpec\` materialization (like \`synthetic_delimiter_format_ppl\`)? The latter avoids a new HF dataset repo and revision pin.
2. **Vocab-coverage size**: Marin tokenizer is ~100k tokens. One row per non-special id ≈ 100k rows for that slice alone. OK as the spec reads, but should we cap at a stratified sample (e.g. all unique tokens by frequency decile) to keep the bundle within \`max_docs_per_dataset=256\`? If kept at full coverage, the bundle needs a per-slice \`max_docs_per_dataset\` override.
3. **Python REPL surface**: scope to single-line \`>>> expr\` continuations, or include multi-line tracebacks / \`...\` continuations?

Implementation is straightforward and well-scoped once (1)-(3) are decided. Happy to proceed once confirmed.

spillover_issues.body:
Issue is to describe the Hero Run scaling ladder, config, and track its performance.

Tracking: https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/reports/535B-A23B-18T-Token-Hero-Run-Scaling-Ladder--VmlldzoxNzc2MDM5Ng

Details on the full model spec is in the comment below.

### Why run a scaling ladder?

1. This lets us project the model performance and compare it to the scaling projections of our prior recipes. If our projection looks meaningfully worse, then we know we need to go back to the drawing board on some aspect of the model or data. This step can catch a lot of bugs!
2. We can look at how training dynamics change as we scale, in particular the gradient norms and token dropping. In our last run, the scaling ladder caught gradient norm growth to over 4 as we scaled out token horizon, which caused us to find a fix with logit z loss. Later ablations showed that without this fix, runs under certain conditions like high batch size would completely blow up mid-run.
3. We can project our evals across the entire trajectory of the run. This means that across the entire ~100 day run, we know exactly how we are doing compared to the projection. If at any point we fail to match the projection, it can prompt early investigation into training dynamics.
4. If something strange start to happen in the Hero run, we can reference the smaller scales runs to see if its actually normal. For instance, in prior scaling ladders we saw the grad norm grow heavily up to 40% of the run, then decrease as the LR decays. When we saw this on the hero run, having the small scale reference gave us confidence we didn't need to intervene, as long as the gradient followed the same pattern (steady growth for 40% of run).
5. It only costs 1% of total compute.
### What is our EP hardware implementation?
Described in detail here: https://storage.googleapis.com/marin-public/rav/moe-fixed-wave-a2a-384/2026.08.17/index.html.
We are hand-rolling our own EP implementation, props to @ravwojdyla, since we have not found a more performant variant on JAX XLA on GPU. 

### What is our long context extension plan?
Our last run was 8k seqlen pretrain, followed by 65k extension for 1T tokens, followed by 262k extension (to occur end of Aug). Prior to that run we have used 4k seqlen pretrain. For this run we are going back to 4k seqlen pretrain to start, to enable better expert balancing (twice as many sequences per batch). We wanted to minimize risk here because our EP token dropping implementation is more experimental. (our last run was dropless FSDP). Prior tests showed token dropping grow from ~7% to ~40% when extending from 4k to 65k seqlen. Our new pooled/wave EP drops about half as many tokens (3%) at 4k seqlen; however the token dropping is likely still excessively high at 65k seqlen.

We will spend 1-2 days to do an early cooldown at roughly 10-20 days into the run, to enable RL experiments, which will be our first full scale data point at how longer context influences dropping. A nice property of this test is that the cooldown will not contaminate or impact the main run, so we have some flexibility to collect data on how an extension approach impacts dropping. Our options will be:
1. If we have landed a Jax Mixture of Kittens or dropless ragged all-to-all, then we can swap to that for the cooldown. Prior small scale tests showed the model was robust from swapping from small amounts of dropping (5%) to dropless mid-run.
2. Otherwise, we can increase our capacity factor, and accept some amount of dropping.
3. If we find that neither of these options are suitable, the next option would be to introduce sequence level balancing mid-run (though forcing the experts to re-specialize mid-run will likely be worse than accepting some amount of dropping). 

Extending context will involve updating qk_mult according to mscale=X⋅ln(new_seqlen/old_seqlen)+1, testing coefficients near 0.1 (can quickly eval a range during extension on 1 rack). If the data from the first cooldown looks smooth, will plan on 4k->8k at 50 pct into run, then 8k->65k at about 95 pct, then a targeted 262k phase near end, based on data we collect from taking the 67B-A2B from 65k to 262k.

Have further derisked token dropping by staying at 2 shared experts, each at half width. 8 active experts are also at half width. However due to latent MoE 2x compression on active experts, we are effectively running at hidden_dim width neurons shared, and 2x hidden_dim neurons routed. Having 1/3 of our neurons come from shared expert will provide a stronger backbone in the event of high dropping. We see learning still progress with zero loss spikes even at 40 pct dropping.

### What if we see delays, beyond our buffer (hardware failure, MFU degradation)?
Up to roughly 25% of the token budget, the default approach will be to compensate by decreasing the token horizon of the run. Since we are using linear LR decay, we would update the decay rate to still reach 0.05 peak at whatever the new horizon point is, and update the datamix.

comments.body:
🤖 # Job Summary: Aug Hero Run — 535B-A23B MoE (d6144), 18T tokens

Full-scale EP64 MoE pretrain: d6144, **535.3B total / 22.76B active** params, **18.0T tokens** (~**2.70e24** train FLOPs, fwd+bwd), on GB200 with our hand-rolled pooled-wave expert-parallel all-to-all. Data is the two-phase Harrier mixture on the fuzzy-deduped datakit store. Below: model, optimizer, training/topology, the MFU optimizations, the scaling ladder, and outputs.

## 1. Model

### Hyperparameters
| | |
|---|---|
| hidden_dim | 6144 |
| num_layers | 48 |
| num_heads | 48 · head_dim 128 |
| num_kv_heads | 12 stored — **local 12 / global 6** (GQA 4:1 local, 8:1 global) |
| num_experts / top-k | **384 / 8** |
| intermediate_dim (expert FFN) | 3072 (= hidden/2) |
| latent_dim (LatentMoE) | 3072 (= hidden/2) |
| shared experts | 2 dense SwiGLU, width 3072 |
| vocab_size | 128,256 |
| max_seq_len | 4096 · sliding_window 2048 · global_every 4 |
| capacity_factor / transport cf | 1.15 / 1.15 · num_expert_waves 3 |
| qk_mult | 1.3 · rope θ=10000 (fused, half-RoPE) |
| sconv | sites k/attn/mlp, kernel 4 |
| init | 0.5/√hidden = 0.006379 (uniform, truncated normal) |
| active / total params | 22.76B / 535.3B |

### Features
All structural (always on) unless noted.
- **All-MoE**: every block's MLP is a QB-routed `MoEMLP`; no dense-only layers.
- **GQA, split local/global KV**: sliding-window (local) layers keep 12 KV heads, full-causal (global) layers 6; K/V are sliced/aligned per layer via `lax.cond`, so global layers pay less KV compute.
- **QB routing (histogram estimator)**: router takes top-(K+1) on biased logits; the (K+1)-th logit is the per-token threshold `alpha`, the first K are selected. Each expert's threshold `beta` is the **(1−K/E) upper quantile of the margins `score−alpha`**, read from a **10k-bin histogram over the live global `[min, max]` range** (a `pmin`/`pmax` this step sets the grid; a summed-histogram cumulative count gives the per-expert quantile). The router bias `−beta` is applied on the **next step** as a zero-mean stop-gradient offset — balances expert selection without touching gradients. The histogram estimator is a smoother global quantile than a per-device top-k.
- **Sigmoid combine weights**: combine weights are `sigmoid(unbiased selected logits)`, rescaled so the K weights sum to a fixed 2.5 (not softmax).
- **LatentMoE + learnable latent RMS-norm**: tokens are compressed `hidden→latent (3072)`, passed through a **learnable RMSNorm (`latent_norm`, per-dim gain)** to decouple the expert-input scale from the down-projection init, then dispatched to experts **entirely in latent space**, and projected `latent→hidden` after the weighted combine. The router still reads the full-width token. (Also halves the all-to-all payload — see §4.)
- **Shared experts**: 2 dense SwiGLU experts run on every token in parallel with the routed path; their output is added before the residual.
- **RMSNorm on embeddings and readout**: a learnable-gain [`RMSNorm`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/12d8b6f09f96ad4f0277445765c1a00dbc81d5be/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/model.py#L594) is applied to the token embeddings ([`embed_norm`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/12d8b6f09f96ad4f0277445765c1a00dbc81d5be/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/model.py#L1223)) and before the untied `lm_head` ([`final_norm`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/12d8b6f09f96ad4f0277445765c1a00dbc81d5be/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/model.py#L1165)), in addition to the per-block `rms_attn`/`rms_mlp`; the GatedNorm below wraps each of these.
- **GatedNorm**: learnable `x·sigmoid(silu(x·w_down)·w_up)` gate (rank-128 bottleneck) applied after **every** RMSNorm (attn, mlp, embed, final).
- **XSA (Exclusive Self-Attention)**: per head, subtract the component of the attention output parallel to its own value vector: `z = y − (yᵀv/‖v‖²)v` — removes the copy-through component so each head learns new information rather than passing V unchanged.
- **Attention head gate**: each head's attention output is scaled by a learned `2·sigmoid(x·attn_gate)`, one scalar per head; `attn_gate` is zero-initialized (gate starts at 1).
- **RMS qk-norm**: Q and K are RMS-normed (non-parametric) per head before RoPE.
- **Partial (half) RoPE, fused**: rotary is applied to **only the first half of head_dim**; the second half is rope-free on every layer. Single-pass fused kernel (θ=10000).
- **Rope-free global layers**: every 4th layer + the last are full-causal and **rope-free** (NoPE, qk_mult-only); the others are sliding-window with RoPE. One per-layer boolean drives mask, KV-head count, and rope together.
- **ShortConv (SConv)**: depthwise causal 1-D conv (kernel 4), identity-init, packed-document segment-masked, at three sites — after K, on the attention-branch output, on the MoE-branch output.
- **Embeddings**: `token_embed` fully replicated + shard-local lookup; `lm_head` (`output_proj`) FSDP+model-sharded; **untied**.
- **Logit z-loss**: the final-logit logsumexp is penalized (`logsumexp_weight = z_loss_weight = 1e-4`) and **added to the training loss** (fused into the CE) — controls gradient-norm growth at long token horizons (the fix the prior scaling ladder surfaced). Distinct from the router z-loss, which is logging-only.
- **Monitoring** (logged, not in loss): per-layer routing entropy, load-balance loss, router z-loss, and sender/receiver token-drop fractions.

## 2. Optimizer — MuonH / AdamH / Adam (compute-scaled)

Three groups via `optax.multi_transform` + a path mask:
- **MuonH** — attention, expert-MLP, shared-expert, latent, and GatedNorm **matrices**. Newton–Schulz orthogonalization (bf16, `backend_steps=5`, quintic coeffs, nesterov momentum 0.95) → **Frobenius-hyperball** scale-invariant step (moves along the direction, projects back onto the param's Frobenius sphere; norms in fp32). Orthogonalization is distributed **intra-rack only** (never crosses DCN); 4D expert stacks are handled without gathering the matrix dims.
- **AdamH** — the **lm_head readout**: Adam moments give the direction, then the same norm-preserving hyperball projection. Gets the MuonH LR, not `adam_lr`.
- **Adam** — `token_embed`, router, router_bias, `attn_gate`, 1-D norm gains, and the tiny SConv kernels.

### Hyperparameters (@ 18T budget)
| | |
|---|---|
| MuonH LR | 0.003291 |
| Adam LR | 0.000759 (MuonH = 13/3 × Adam = 4.33×) |
| beta1 / beta2 | **0.90** / 0.95 |
| epsilon | 6.04e-15 (Adam) · muon_epsilon 1e-8 |
| momentum / nesterov | 0.95 / true |
| use_syrk | true (Blackwell SM100 symmetric GEMM for X·Xᵀ) |
| LR schedule | linear · warmup 1% · min_lr_ratio 0.05 |
| max_grad_norm | none (no global clip) |
| z_loss_weight | 1e-4 (logit z-loss, fused into CE) |

The MuonH/AdamH groups carry **no decoupled weight decay** — they regularize purely through the norm-preserving hyperball projection. LR / beta2 / epsilon are compute-scaled from the Aug hero refit (issues #7856 / #8003, R²=0.978, seq_len=8192): `adam_lr = 0.087571 · tokens^-0.3461 · hidden^-0.3448 · √(tokens_per_batch)`, `beta2 = clip(0.999^(tpb/131072), 0.95, 0.9999)`, `epsilon = 9.676e-18 · √(tokens/tpb)`.

## 3. Training & topology
- **Hardware**: 11× GB200 NVL72 racks. **EP64 within each rack** (expert axis = 16 nodes × 4 GPUs), **data-parallel replication across the 11 racks over DCN**. Mesh `(replica_dcn=11, data, expert=64, model)`; token/batch sharded over `(replica_dcn, data, expert)`.
- **batch_size** 11,264 seqs (1024 × 11 racks) · **seq_len** 4096 · **num_train_steps** 390,139 · **total_tokens 18.0T** · **791 tokens/active-param**.
- **compute_budget** ≈ 2.70e24 FLOPs (analytic, fwd+bwd, latent-corrected).
- **mixed_precision** `params=bf16, compute=bf16, output=bf16`, with **fp32 pinned-host master params** + **offloaded optimizer state** (see §4). Router path kept fp32 before top-k/softmax/QB stats.
- **data**: two-phase Harrier mixture (15T pretrain + 3.75T cooldown, phase-1 at 80% of steps) on the fuzzy-deduped datakit store, marin tokenizer; simulated epoching against the 18.75T reference with a ≤8-epoch cap (max cell exposure ~2.1). 4k-seq pretrain deliberately (2× sequences/batch for expert balancing; token-drop grows sharply at longer context).

## 4. MFU / performance optimizations
- **Hand-rolled fixed pooled-wave all-to-all EP** — every device packs sends into one fixed `[expert_shards, pool_capacity]` pool and receives into fixed per-wave `[local_experts, receiver_cap, H]` buffers; all sizes are compile-time constants so the `all_to_all` runs on fully static shapes. Chosen over `ragged_all_to_all` to avoid a metadata/offset collective and dynamic shapes; **expert IDs ride in-band** as packed header rows in the same activation collective (no separate metadata collective). [EP writeup](https://storage.googleapis.com/marin-public/rav/moe-fixed-wave-a2a-384/2026.08.17/index.html)
- **Static waves (3)** stripe each destination pool round-robin by rank, shrinking per-wave buffers; each wave is rematerialized to cap activation memory. **Round-robin receiver allocation** keeps overflow drops unbiased across senders.
- **LatentMoE halves EP transport bytes** — the all-to-all carries latent-width (3072) rows both directions instead of hidden (6144). FLOP accounting is corrected for this so MFU isn't overstated.
- **gpu_fa4_cute FA4 attention** — bf16 CuTe segmented flash attention with per-token key lower bounds (no materialized `[B,S,S]` mask, no THD compaction), real GQA, custom CUTLASS backward, grug-tuned 64×64 tiles for B200/head_dim-128. **Sliding-window vs full-causal is just a different lower-bound array feeding the same kernel** → cuts attention FLOPs on the ~3/4 local layers. Bounds are precomputed **outside** the layer scan.
- **Fused linear-softmax cross-entropy (bf16 backward)** — `implementation="xla_fast_bwd"`: streams the whole 65,536-token rank shard over `v_block=4096` vocab blocks with online logsumexp (never materializes the `[B,128k]` logits), and runs both **backward GEMMs in bf16 on tensor cores** (vs fp32/TF32) for ~2.3× on the hero CE shape; the logit z-loss is fused as `logsumexp_weight·lse²`. `v_block=4096` is the dominant MFU lever for the 128k vocab.
- **Fused depthwise causal ShortConv (Pallas)** — the SConv sites dispatch to a fused **Pallas Triton depthwise causal conv** kernel on GPU (forward and `dx` bit-identical to the pad-and-shift reference, `dw` as accurate; pad-and-shift fallback off-GPU). Shard-local (depthwise, no cross-channel/cross-shard term → no collectives); the channel dim is FSDP-sharded so its gradient reduce-scatters.
- **Muon symmetric-GEMM (QuACK SM100) Newton–Schulz** — the two `X·Xᵀ` products in each Newton–Schulz iteration go through a **QuACK symmetric CuTe GEMM** (`use_syrk`) that computes only one triangle of the symmetric output (`A = X·Xᵀ`, then `B = b·A + c·(A·Aᵀ)`) instead of a full dense matmul — roughly halves the matmul FLOPs per iteration on the batched 4D expert stacks, where orthogonalization is the bulk of the optimizer's compute.
- **Padded + resharded distributed Muon (intra-rack)** — the stacked leaves are orthogonalized in parallel across the rack instead of gathered to one device: 3D non-expert stacks **zero-pad the leading (layer) axis** so it divides the intra-rack shard count, then reshard the padded stack over the batch mesh axes (one matrix per shard, `vmap`'d, resliced back after); 4D expert stacks `[layers, experts, fan_in, fan_out]` reshard over the `expert` axis (or the largest batch-axis subset that divides `layers·experts`) and run under a `shard_map` **without ever gathering the `fan_in×fan_out` matrix dims**, then reshard back to the parameter's own spec. All of this is pinned **intra-rack only** — the reshards deliberately exclude the `replica_dcn` axis so Newton–Schulz never runs a collective over the slow inter-rack DCN link.
- **ArrayStacked + `jax.lax.scan`** — all 48 blocks are one compiled body scanned over the layer axis, cutting compile time and HBM; router/QB collectives are structured around the scan.
- **Heterogeneous global/local layers under one homogeneous scan** — `lax.scan` needs a single compiled body, so the ways global (full-causal, rope-free) and local (sliding-window) layers differ can't be Python branches — each rides in as a traced per-layer scalar and is selected *inside* the body:
  - **RoPE diff** — global layers run rope-free. Rather than branch, RoPE is **always computed** and then selected with `jnp.where` on a per-layer `disable_rope` scalar, so both layer kinds compile to the same body.
  - **GQA diff** — local layers keep 12 KV heads, global layers 6. K/V are stored at the max (12) width and sliced-then-`align_kv_heads`'d to the per-layer count via `lax.cond(is_global, …)`, so global layers pay less KV compute without changing the stacked parameter shape.
  - **Mask diff** — the full-causal and sliding-window FA4 bound arrays are precomputed **outside** the scan and the per-layer one is picked with `jnp.where` (the sliding window is a static mask field the body can't vary), so the window rides in as the selected bounds.
- **remat `recompute_all`** — the whole block is recomputed in backward (lowest memory); a `save_moe` mode is available to keep the MoE dispatch tensors and skip re-running the EP collectives.
- **Capacity-factor token dropping (1.15)** bounds expert compute and transport buffers regardless of routing imbalance; drops are counted/logged as sender/receiver fractions.
- **use_syrk** routes the optimizer's `X·Xᵀ` through QuACK's SM100 symmetric GEMM; Newton–Schulz runs in bf16 (halved all-gather bytes) and **intra-rack only**.
- **offload_opt_state + FP32_PINNED_HOST master** — optimizer state and fp32 master weights live in pinned host RAM, shuttled device↔host each step, to leave HBM for the pooled all-to-all buffers. (The pinned-host restore is fixed in [#8443](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/8443) and memory-bounded in [#8480](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/8480); the hero now writes an hourly temporary checkpoint and resumes from it after a preemption.)
- **XLA/runtime flags** — latency-hiding scheduler on, collective-overlap limit 4, CUDA async allocator, 192GB host-memory limit, PGLE off, GPU command buffers disabled.

## 5. Scaling ladder (why, and the rungs)
Runs at 5 widths on one iso-ratio recipe (**791 tokens/active-param**, same mixture + simulated epoching + per-cell epoch structure), ≈1% of total compute, to (a) project performance vs prior recipes and catch bugs, (b) watch grad-norm and token-drop dynamics across scale (the last ladder caught grad-norm growth → the logit z-loss fix), and (c) project evals across the ~100-day trajectory.

| rung | racks | batch | steps | tokens | active |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| d768 | 1 | 1024 | 11,420 | 48B | 61M |
| d1024 | 2 | 2048 | 15,276 | 128B | 162M |
| d1536 | 6 | 6144 | 15,128 | 381B | 481M |
| d2048 | 11 | 11,264 | 20,072 | 926B | 1.2B |
| **d6144 (hero)** | 11 | 11,264 | 390,139 | **18.0T** | 22.8B |

comments.author: Helw150
comments.body:
## Raw Data

On the raw data side, our pool for this hero run is logged at this frozen commit of [our data provenance table on hugging face](https://huggingface.co/datasets/marin-community/token-counts/commit/3612ddc3350212e38ce8a50b99c3df7ea10b44a9). The raw (pre-dedupe) pool contains 25.6 trillion tokens from 292 sources (though >100 of those are a variety of rollout datasets courtesy of @penfever!).

## Deduplication & Decontamination

For this run, we removed 2.494T tokens through a combination of  fuzzy deduplication and n-gram based decontamination w.r.t many common benchmarks in LM-eval-harness + the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index (~250k documents were removed) for a final count of 23.106T tokens. 

Fuzzy duplication used a combination of MinHash deduplication and heuristics among linked pairs within connected component clusters. Examples of duplicates can be found here: https://storage.googleapis.com/marin-public/rav/dedup-pair-browser/2026.08.18.2/index.html

## Bucketing

We then embedded all documents with [Harrier 0.6b](https://huggingface.co/microsoft/harrier-oss-v1-0.6b). 

For topic labels, documents were grouped into 40 semantic buckets by first performing K-means with 5000 clusters (using a sample of 2.56 Million documents) and then doing agglomerative clustering over those 500 clusters to get 40 buckets.

For quality labels, documents were labeled using GLM 5.2 for quality and these labels were distilled into a "Faster Transformer" classifier using both the harrier embedding and the token distribution of the document.

You can see samples from each bucket + distributions from source -> topic x document buckets here: https://storage.googleapis.com/marin-public/held/harrier-k40-cluster-overview/2026.08.18/index.html?revision=uniform-sampling

comments.body:
🤖 Scaling-ladder analysis for the **535B-A23B, 18T-token** hero. The ladder trains one uniform hero EP recipe at five widths; four rungs finished and the d2048 rung crashed at ~81%. Fitting a power law across the rungs (`L = 1.5 + A·C^-α`, compute excludes lm_head) and extrapolating to the hero's compute predicts a final **dropless paloma macro-loss ≈ 2.04**.

**Hero prediction by training percentile** — the four measured rungs plus the d6144 hero prediction at every 5% (dashed/hollow = extrapolated).
![hero prediction by percentile](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/marin-community/marin/d23e6e9c3673435fb82d83aa6c51a607d0da6009/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/scaling_ladder_figs/hero_prediction_by_percentile.png)

**Per-5% scaling-law fits (log-log)** — one power-law fit per training fraction; the crimson points trace the hero prediction out to hero-scale compute, ending at 2.039 @100%.
![scaling law fits](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/marin-community/marin/d23e6e9c3673435fb82d83aa6c51a607d0da6009/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/scaling_ladder_figs/ladder_scaling_laws.png)

**Method check** — a linear extrapolation from each finished rung's 60–80% window predicts its own 100% dropless macro-loss to within ~0.003–0.004 (consistently a hair optimistic, since the curve flattens under cosine decay).
![60-80 extrapolation vs actual](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/marin-community/marin/d23e6e9c3673435fb82d83aa6c51a607d0da6009/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/scaling_ladder_figs/ladder_extrapolation_60_80.png)

**Full-granularity training cross-entropy** — every step, with the datamix phase-2 boundary at 80% (a small loss bump is visible in every rung at that point).
![training cross-entropy](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/marin-community/marin/d23e6e9c3673435fb82d83aa6c51a607d0da6009/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/scaling_ladder_figs/ladder_train_ce_fullres.png)

Prior precedent for this kind of extrapolation — the 67B-A2B 10T run's preregistered (80%) and two retroactive (21%, 63%) scaling-law fits each predicted that run's target within ~0.6% (issue #6044):
![67B scaling fits](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/marin-community/marin/d23e6e9c3673435fb82d83aa6c51a607d0da6009/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/scaling_ladder_figs/scaling_fit_67b_prereg_vs_retro.png)

Full source to reproduce (pulls the W&B runs and regenerates the ladder figures): [`experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/plot_scaling_ladder.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/d23e6e9c3673435fb82d83aa6c51a607d0da6009/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/plot_scaling_ladder.py).

comments.author: ClassicLarry
comments.body: Comparing our scaling law to prior runs. The main differences here is that the May recipe is at compute optimal, this run is at ~12x overtrained, and the 67B-A2B scaling law was at 100x overtrained. The 67B-A2B ran at 8k seqlen, and was therefore given a lower asympotote of 1.4 instead of 1.5. The May fit also inaccurately has an asympotote at 1.6 instead of 1.5. Main architecture change is we dropped from 4/256 level of sparsity to 4/192 level of sparsity (25% fewer total parameters, to fit on GB200 at this scale. Several other small features added. Overall, the scaling law looks reasonable and nothing looks off in the training dynamics or data. Grad norms look stable over the run, peaking at 25% into the run. These runs ran at oversized batch sizes, which may be slightly suppressing the gradient. Expecting the grad norm to climb higher on the hero run, but still peak at the same ~25% into the run. This will be good metric to monitor for issues. Drop rate jumps to 10 pct at very start, then drops to 0, then climbs to ~4pct over the run. Slightly increasing as we scale. Predicting we wont have that 10 percent spike for the hero, because our warmup (1 percent) will cover a much larger number of steps since the hero is at a higher step count. comments.author: ClassicLarry
comments.body:
From model perspective, main risk points during the run:

1. First 3%. Can we get through LR warmup and reach steady dynamics? If we see gradient run away/large issues here, we likely need to revisit initialization, or potentially initial batch size. Or increase capacity factor if the issue involves high dropping.
2. 30% mark. Gradient may peak, and we will see if gradient keeps climbing, or if its starts to cooldown. Indication that it keeps climbing indefinitely could indicate we need stronger logit z loss, lower token dropping, or revisit some of the norm constraints.
3. Context Extension. How will token dropping respond? See initial Issue desc.
4. Very low loss regime. If training plateaus or acts strange near end of run only, first things to check will be the numerics.

Health checklist:

1. Is total grad norm oscillating steadily? In our May 16B active run, the grad norm grew steadily to 1.5 and training was still very smooth. So I am less concerned with the absolute magnitude, and more concerned with the rate of change. Hyperball makes comparing absolute magnitude not apples to apples with AdamW runs.
2. Are all Hyberball constrained parameters actually respecting the constraint? In past we have seen bug where JAX does norm calculation incorrectly, due to some transient sharding issue. This has been updated to a more explicit calculation that seemed to resolve that issue, but issues of a similar nature may arise.
3. Is token dropping following similar trend as scaling ladder?
4. Is loss decreasing steadily?
5. Are evals decreasing steadily?
6. Is our router bias terms behaving steadily?
7. Does router entropy stay near max?
8. Is embed norm growth reasonable?
9. Is MFU holding constant?
10. Is LR schedule (both Adam and MuonH params) actually following the correct schedule?
11. Does the entire wandb config look accurate?
12. Are we hitting the projected eval targets at each 5 percent?

Thanks for sharing this work.  
I have a question regarding the motivation behind LatentMoE. Since the training system uses GB200 NVL72 with high-bandwidth NVLink, I am curious why a latent representation is introduced before expert dispatch.

comments.author: ClassicLarry
comments.body:
> Thanks for sharing this work. I have a question regarding the motivation behind LatentMoE. Since the training system uses GB200 NVL72 with high-bandwidth NVLink, I am curious why a latent representation is introduced before expert dispatch. Is LatentMoE mainly motivated by reducing communication overhead at larger scales (e.g., beyond a single NVLink domain), or does it also provide benefits beyond communication optimization, such as improving model capability? Thanks!

On its own, LatentMoE halves the comms cost. We found that putting a learnable RMSNorm on the latent projection improved model capability as well, so LatentMoE w/ norm performed better than no latent MoE. Without this learnable RMSNorm, we run into activation scaling issue and see 30 percent worse quality. We also found going from top 4 of 192 to top 8 of 384 (half sized) gave 15 percent quality gain. But it doubles comms cost. So one way to view latentMoE is it enables 4/192->8/384 without change to either comms or compute.

comments.body: > Thanks for the detailed reply! I have a few follow-up questions after looking through some of the previous Marin experiments. 1. MAI Thinking makes their dense layers only have num_neurons = hidden_dim, which is roughly 3x smaller than normal. This to me a is a bit awkward at first glance because attn is still full capacity every layer. So the normal behavior of attention fetch info, mlp process it is a bit imbalanced (of course if one has data that an idea is good, that it seeming awkward doesn't matter, but it made me more hesitant to spend the time collecting that data instead of working on other things). At very small scale if I do an exact active:total replica (dense 3x width hidden instead of 1x), I get same quality and 20% better MFU than our baseline. I am less optimistic about alternating dense/moe long term, because with mature mixture-of-kittens kernels the MFU hit of MoE is probably not that high anyways. 2. Hmm I separately saw some early positive results from Inkling relative position embedding that gave lower loss. But our kernel was not quite fast enough to justify. And perhaps more importantly, the kernel was a bit buggy if I changed sliding window length. I think it should be good on global layers too, since its limited to just the most recent X (512 or 1024) positions. I am more bullish on relative position embedding + MLA. Since MLA has very janky approach to RoPE, which requires replicating 64 head dims across every head. Relative position embedding fixes this. Have to be a bit careful with ablations here because at very small scale RoPE on global looks much better than NoPE on global. (but this fades with scale) 3. So initial AdamH on embed looked good. But later I did learning rate sweep, and if LR was 40% too high, was seeing grad spikes up to 20. I think what was happening (guessing) was rare tokens were having their norm driven to near zero, and then getting massive grad when they finally ended up in the batch. (we have rms_norm on embed that will apply high growth multiplier to small vocab embeds) Dont want any features in the model that require perfectly optimal hypers. So reverted it.

comments.author: MythosAd
comments.body:
Thanks, this is really helpful.

My motivation for alternating dense/MoE is less about the current MFU gap and more about separation of concerns: dense layers handle common computation, while MoE layers handle specialization. Keeping them as two clean execution patterns seems to leave more room for independent kernel, scheduling, and parallelism optimization, even if MoE kernels improve substantially.

For position encoding, my preference for learned relative PE on local layers + NoPE on global layers is mainly to avoid positional extrapolation entirely. With a fixed local window, the relative-position range never changes as context grows, while global attention stays purely content-addressed. I agree this probably needs larger-scale ablations to judge properly.

🤖 Layer-skip ablation on the step-42k checkpoint — dropless macro loss with whole transformer layers dropped from the forward (restored on one rack, scored with the hero's own dropless evaluator).

| ablation | layers run | dropless macro loss | Δ vs baseline |
|---|---|---:|---:|

comments.author: ClassicLarry
comments.body:
Summarizing findings:
1. At hero_scale attention gate shows uncharacteristic increase in norm. 
2. The 48 heads of the attention gate show high cosine similarity on any given layer. Checking layer zero, 98 percent of the time the attention gate is driving attention down to under 5 percent of its initial output scale.
3. Contributions to the residual stream scale with layer depth. MLP tends to contribute about 2x more than attention. Layer zero contributes about 1/10 the norm of the initial embed. Layer 48 contributes about 10x the norm of the initial embed. 
4. However zeroing out attention on the first 10 layers causes a meaningful increase in loss. A greater increase (2x) than zeroing out attention on the last 10 layers. So attention in early layers is still contributing very meaningfully. (changes from attention in early layers influence what updates later layers make). This contribution should act as a 'tether' that prevents these layers from becoming useless. (the gradient would yell very loudly if attention gate turned them off completely). Main learning: output scale does not correspond to impact.

Suspicion is that the attn_gate parameter has been co-opted in early layers to function as an output scaling mechanism. The intention was for the input RMSNorm on the attn block to handle this, or the sconv on attn_out.

Given that the first 10 attn layers are still critical and actively getting used (just smaller scale outputs), not viewing as issue that requires immediate action. Things would prompt intervention:
1. Loss curve slows down and no longer beats projection.
2. Ablating removing early attention layers actually shows no impact on loss later on in training.
3. We get positive results from an ablation on 1 rack that resumes from checkpoint, when compared to baseline:

Ablation ideas:
1. Update attention gate from v = 2*sigmoid(x)*v to v = (0.05 + 2*sigmoid(x))*v. Give nonzero floor.
2. Instead of hardcoded 0.05, make it a learnable bias per head with very high beta1 and beta2. Init to 0.
3. Add a general output scalar on each attn output. Init to 1 with very high beta1 and beta2.
4. Add some regularization to attn gate weight (weight decay).
5. Add hardcoded bias that ramps per step from 0 to 0.05 over 1000 steps.

All of these ablation ideas would probably not be effective as-is. But testing on 1 rack would give signal and better intuition on how the system is behaving. Since attention gate runs through a sigmoid, it would never fully decay to zero. Since this dynamic only occurs on hero scale (48 layers), all ablations would need to occur there.

comments.author: ClassicLarry
comments.body:
Main initial concern here was that gradient signal to the attention matrices would be getting killed by attn gate being off. But actually, the gradient signal is likely still reasonable, its just that model has adopted a behavior where output scale grows with depth (but early layers still impact prediction heavily through their impact on subsequent layers), and this depth scaling is managed partially by the attention gate, perhaps partially because matrices are under hyperball. Will be important to get per-layer gradient logging on Hero to track this more actively. (scan layers is bundling the gradient across all layers).

Traditionally the intent of residual highway is it gives direct gradient signal back from lm_head to every layer directly. However since we see output scale of every layer increase, the early layers will influence prediction very little through direct residual highway. Instead, their influence comes from how they influence subsequent layers. This seems like it would perhaps be less stable. Though training seems extremely stable so far? As long as gradient on attention matrices in initial layers looks ok, then biasing towards no action.

comments.author: ClassicLarry
comments.body:
🤖 Layer-0 headwise attention gate, per-vocab-token (step-42000). The gate is `2·sigmoid(attn_in @ attn_gate)`, one value per head (48 heads); at layer 0 `attn_in` is a deterministic function of the token embedding, so each token has a fixed 48-head gate vector. "On" = gate > 1 (i.e. `attn_in @ attn_gate > 0`).

Layer-0 attention is near-closed by default: mean gate over the whole vocab is **0.013**. Only **546 of 128,256 tokens open ≥1 head**, and just **93 open all 48**. The tokens that stay on fall into three buckets:

**1. Reserved/special tokens (128000–128255)** — the bulk. ~200 of the 256 special tokens open all 48 heads (opensum 96/96): `<|reserved_special_token_*|>` plus the structural specials (`<|begin_of_text|>`, `<|end_of_text|>`, `<|eot_id|>`).

**2. Malformed / byte-fragment real-vocab tokens** — the top non-special tokens are almost all junk:
- undecodable UTF-8 byte fragments that decode to `�` (ids 124, 125, 178–187), several at the full 96/96
- rare foreign-script subwords: Turkish (`ıldığında`, `ılmaz`, `uştur`, `ılmaktadır`), Cyrillic/Ukrainian (`уватися`, `илася`, `аракт`), Czech (`ujícím`), CJK spam strings (`菲律宾申博`, `갤로그로`)
- gibberish/spam: `eoqkrvldkf`, `.:.:.:.:.:.:`, `.**************`, `ЎыџN`

**3. Ordinary English text tokens** — essentially none; common words sit at gate ≈ 0.

Distribution of open-head counts (real-vocab tokens only, excluding the special block): 345 open ≥1 head, 32 open ≥12 heads.

## TL;DR

The final Hero forecast is 0.7406 Paloma BPB. Nemotron 3 Super-120B-A12B-Base measures 0.7918 BPB, Qwen3.5-35B-A3B-Base measures 0.8397 BPB, and Nemotron 3 Nano-30B-A3B-Base measures 0.8846 BPB. The Hero forecast is 6.5% lower than Super, 11.8% lower than Qwen, and 16.3% lower than Nano. It is lower than Super on 14 of 16 Paloma subsets.

![Hero and three open-weight models by Paloma subset](https://storage.googleapis.com/marin-public/held/hero-open-weight-ppl/2026.08.31.4/paloma-subset-forecasts.png)

## Description

Compare Hero with open-weight base models on the same evaluation data. Report bits per byte (BPB) because token perplexity is not comparable across tokenizers.

## Hypothesis or Goal

Measure each base model with the Hero evaluation protocol. Add each result to the same comparison.

## Status

| Model | Paloma BPB | UncheatableEval BPB |
|---|---:|---:|
| Hero final forecast | 0.7406 | — |
| Nemotron 3 Super-120B-A12B-Base | 0.7918 | 0.4964 |
| Hero without token dropping, step 45,837 | 0.8188 | 0.5362 |
| Hero with token dropping, step 45,837 | 0.8868 | 0.6220 |
| Qwen3.5-35B-A3B-Base | 0.8397 | 0.5245 |
| Nemotron 3 Nano-30B-A3B-Base | 0.8846 | 0.5703 |

Nano and Super use the full 15-subset UncheatableEval. The Hero and Qwen values use the earlier 7-subset suite, so those UncheatableEval values are not directly comparable with Nano and Super.

Each subset forecast fits BPB as a function of Paloma macro-loss across 77 paired ladder measurements. It then applies the preregistered macro-loss scaling law. Fifteen fits have `R² ≥ 0.997`; Twitter AAE has `R² = 0.971`.

The Hero forecast is 6.6% to 21.6% lower than Qwen and 8.0% to 38.5% lower than Nano across the 16 subsets. It is 1.0% to 40.3% lower than Super on 14 subsets. Super is 5.1% lower on M2D2 Wikipedia and 9.2% lower on WikiText-103.

The FLOP axis uses `6 × active parameters × training tokens` estimates. Super is at `1.8e24` FLOPs from 12B active parameters and 25T tokens. NVIDIA reports over 25T tokens, so this is a lower-bound coordinate. Qwen is at `6.48e23` FLOPs from 3B active parameters and a 36T-token assumption. Nano is at `5.25e23` FLOPs from NVIDIA's published 3.5B active parameters and 25T training tokens. Exact FLOP totals for the hybrid MoE architectures are unknown.

A bootstrap over the four ladder runs gives 0.7404–0.7432 macro BPB. This range covers the loss-to-BPB conversion. It does not cover error in the loss forecast.

The forecast assumes a 4K context, the original data mix, and the planned token count. These inputs can change before training ends. We do not have a final UncheatableEval forecast.

## Decision Log

- 2026-08-31: Limit the final forecast to Paloma. UncheatableEval has no final forecast.
- 2026-09-01: Place Qwen, Nano, and Super on the FLOP axis with labeled 6ND estimates. Super's coordinate is a lower bound because NVIDIA reports over 25T training tokens.

## Conclusion

spillover_issues.author: rjpower
spillover_issues.body:
## TL;DR

Just kicking off: measure whether adaptive environment/problem sampling improves RL training efficiency under a fixed compute budget, versus uniform random sampling.

## Description

We run SkyRL GRPO post-training on a small Qwen policy (0.6B class) over a pool of verifiable, non-agentic environments (math datasets spanning difficulty, plus simple programmatic tasks). Each arm uses the same model, data pool, and budget; only the policy for choosing which environment/problem to roll out next differs.

Arms:

1. Naive sampling: uniform random over the pool (baseline).
2. Modified Thompson sampling: bias toward environments currently yielding reward signal (e.g. per-env reward variance / pass-rate entropy), with decay so the belief tracks policy drift.
3. Pre-graded difficulty (problems graded 0–N easiest→hardest):
   - Naive curriculum: 1/N of budget per level.
   - Adaptive curriculum: train on a level until it stops paying (saturated or not learning), then move.
   - Biased sampling: grades seed an initial belief distribution for the Thompson sampler.

Budget: fixed output-token count per run, falling back to GPU wall-time (64 H100s x fixed hours) if token accounting is impractical. Runs use INTERACTIVE priority on cw-rno2a. The experiment is wired through Marin artifact steps (`marin.rl.skyrl`) so arms are cached and rerunnable; sampler support lands on a MarinSkyRL branch if the pinned trainer lacks the hooks.

## Hypothesis or Goal

Reward-signal-aware sampling concentrates rollouts where the learning signal is, so adaptive arms should reach a given eval score with fewer output tokens than uniform sampling. Quantify the value of each mechanism at fixed budget.

## Status

Kickoff. Wiring the experiment directory and a small smoke run.

Planned milestones, posted as comments:

1. Initial smoke run working end to end.
2. Curriculum/sampling infrastructure wired.
3. Results per sampling arm.
4. Final report on arm efficacy and follow-up recommendations.

## Links

* Logbook:
* W&B Report:
* Important updates:

## Decision Log

## Conclusion

comments.author: rjpower
comments.body:
🤖 Wiring status: the training loop works end to end; the smoke milestone is blocked only on a MarinSkyRL export bug.

What ran: `experiments/post_training/curriculum_rl/` builds a 6-bin graded pool (GSM8K, MATH L1-2/3/4/5, AIME 1983-2024; 10,427 train rows, 756 validation rows), mirrors Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B@c1899de, and runs SkyRL GRPO on 2 nodes of cw-rno2a H100s at interactive priority through `skyrl_step`, with pool/model artifacts cached across attempts. The smoke run completed all 4 GRPO steps over the mixed-env parquet (per-row `env_class`), logging per-environment metrics (train `environment/acc` 0.023 at step 4 — the raw 0.6B policy under a 1024-token cap).

Fixes landed on the branch along the way:

1. MarinSkyRL pin b45a6ed2 crashed at startup (`SKYRL_DEBUG_ARTIFACT_DIR is required`); advanced to d018d672, which contains the upstream fix.
2. The `aime` env asserts `extras["reward_model"]["ground_truth"]` (the gsm8k env reads `reward_spec`); pool rows now carry both columns.
3. The `aime` env verifies with the Minerva `Answer: ...` extraction, not `\boxed{}`; prompts now elicit a final Answer line. Representative ground truths (integers, degrees, fractions, tuples, radicals, polynomials) pass the skyrl-gym contract's two-sided preflight.

Open blocker: at d018d672 the terminal policy export (`cloud.iris.export_hf_checkpoint`) dies with `ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'torch'` — `skyrl_train/hf_export.py` pulls `skyrl_train.utils`, whose package init imports torch, into the deliberately torch-free launcher env. A fix branch (`fix-hf-export-torch-free`: move the torch-free `utils/io` subpackage and checkpoint-listing helpers out of the torch-bound `utils` package) is in progress; next smoke rerun follows it.

Confidence: high that the remaining blocker is isolated to export; the curriculum sampler infrastructure (MarinSkyRL `data.sampling` subtree + stateful weighted sampler) is being implemented in parallel.

comments.author: rjpower
comments.body:
🤖 Milestone 1: the smoke run is green end to end.

`/power/curriculum-rl-smoke-coord-r7` completed the full chain on cw-rno2a: graded-pool build → Qwen3-0.6B mirror → 2-node SkyRL GRPO (4 steps over the mixed six-bin parquet) → terminal HF export (`global_step_4`) → gsm8k-smoke eval, all as cached artifact steps at version 2026.08.29.1. Wall time for the RL step is about 10 minutes; the smoke score itself carries no signal at 4 steps.

Two more MarinSkyRL export bugs surfaced and were fixed on `fix-hf-export-torch-free` (now pinned at 5f6aed2d) beyond the torch-free import: the export subprocess wrote its console output to the launcher's JSON-only stdout, and it resolved the caller-relative cluster config from the wrong working directory. One experiment-side footgun: the launcher auto-defaults `trainer.hf_hub_repo_id` to `laion/<job_name>` and the export 403s creating that repo; arms now override it to null so exports stay in object storage.

Next: land the curriculum sampler branch (in progress), validate the thompson arm at smoke scale, then start the full 64-GPU naive baseline.

comments.author: rjpower
comments.body:
🤖 **Milestone 2: infrastructure wired for curricula & sampling.**

The curriculum sampler is implemented on MarinSkyRL branch [`curriculum-sampling`](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/tree/curriculum-sampling) (@2a9034fd) and validated live: naive, thompson, and grade-adaptive smoke arms all ran green end-to-end (train → HF export → eval) on cw-rno2a.

Design: a `data.sampling` config subtree selects a stateful weighted sampler over the pool's graded bins (`extra_info.data_source` / `grade`). Kinds: `naive` (stock shuffle), `thompson` (Beta posterior on the decay-weighted fraction of *informative* GRPO groups — groups whose rollout rewards are not all equal), `grade-uniform` (equal budget per grade), `grade-adaptive` (train one grade until its informative fraction stays below a threshold for a window, then advance), `grade-prior` (Thompson seeded with grade-derived optimism). The sampler is checkpoint-resumable (torchdata Stateful) and rejects duplicate rows per batch to preserve the GRPO group invariant.

Smoke evidence the machinery works (4-step runs, Qwen3-0.6B, non-thinking):
- thompson: weights collapsed to ~1% on the two bins with zero informative groups (MATH-L5, AIME) and concentrated on informative middle bins.
- grade-adaptive: 80% mass on grade 0 (gsm8k, informative_frac 0.47 — not yet exhausted, level correctly held at 0) with 20% exploration.
- Non-thinking mode fixed the truncation problem: 85% → 20% truncated, 4% → 70% parseable answers, ~500 avg output tokens.

Fixes along the way: unstepped-episode metrics crash, over-length prompts filtered at pool build (8 rows dropped), per-token reward scalarization for the sampler, batch-unique draws.

Next: full-scale arms (64 GPUs, 120 steps × 512 prompts × 8 samples each) starting with the naive baseline.

comments.author: rjpower
comments.body:
🤖 **Results: all five arms complete** (120 GRPO steps each, Qwen3-0.6B, 8×H100x8 per arm, cw-rno2a).

**Fixed output-token budget (146M generated tokens — the smallest arm's total):** last in-run validation eval at or under budget, avg_score on val-math500 / val-gsm8k:

| arm | tokens at eval | val-math500 | val-gsm8k |
|---|---|---|---|
| grade-adaptive | 146M (its full run) | **0.156** | 0.770 |
| thompson | 142M (~57% of run) | 0.140 | 0.758 |
| grade-uniform | 141M | 0.088 | 0.734 |
| naive | 136M (~50% of run) | 0.080 | **0.793** |
| grade-prior | 139M | 0.064 | 0.789 |

**Fixed step count (120 steps, unequal token spend):** terminal Evalchemy on the exported checkpoints:

| arm | total gen tokens | MATH500 acc | gsm8k-0shot (flexible) |
|---|---|---|---|
| naive | 274M | **0.460** | 0.450 |
| thompson | 251M | 0.412 | **0.516** |
| grade-uniform | 285M | 0.430 | 0.375 |
| grade-prior | 253M | 0.428 | 0.449 |
| grade-adaptive | 146M | 0.364 | 0.472 |

Base non-thinking Qwen3-0.6B started near val-math500 ≈ 0 and gsm8k ≈ 0.65, so every arm learns substantially. Wall time was ~1.75h for every arm (generation runs on fixed engine capacity), so fixed-step is also approximately fixed-GPU-hours: 5 arms × 64 GPU × 1.75h.

Reading: curriculum arms buy **token efficiency, not a better endpoint at equal steps**. grade-adaptive matched or beat the mid-run baselines while generating 53% of naive's tokens (it trains mostly on easier, shorter problems until they stop being informative); thompson tracks close behind and reallocates automatically without pre-grading. When the budget is steps/wall-time rather than tokens, naive remains the strongest MATH500 arm and thompson the strongest gsm8k arm.

Caveats: single seed per arm; 0.6B model; in-run val scorer (reward incl. penalties) differs from Evalchemy accuracy; grade-adaptive had not yet advanced past mid grades at 120 steps, so longer runs may shift the picture.

Final report with recommendations follows.

comments.author: rjpower
comments.body:
🤖 **Final report: efficacy and recommendations.**

**Conclusions.**
1. *Curriculum value here is token efficiency, not a better endpoint.* At a fixed generated-token budget (146M), grade-adaptive reached mid-run-baseline quality at ~53% of naive's token spend (val-math500 0.156 vs 0.080), with thompson close behind (0.140). At a fixed step/GPU-hour budget — where generation capacity is already paid for — naive was the best MATH500 arm (0.460) and thompson the best gsm8k arm (0.516); no curriculum dominated naive.
2. *Thompson sampling is the best no-prep default.* No offline grading required, decay handles policy drift, competitive under both budget definitions, and it visibly reallocated: bins with zero informative groups (MATH L5, AIME — all-fail for a 0.6B policy) dropped to the 1% floor.
3. *Grade-prior and grade-uniform added little* — the grade-derived prior washes out once real reward evidence accumulates, and fixed 1/N allocation wastes budget on uninformative extremes.

**Recommendations.**
- Re-run naive / thompson / grade-adaptive at 3 seeds for error bars before production conclusions (~$3 × current spend; each arm is 64 GPUs × 1.75 h).
- Extend grade-adaptive to 300+ steps so it traverses all grades; its curve was still rising at half the token budget.
- Make thompson difficulty-directional (distinguish all-pass from all-fail groups) — that should recover grade-adaptive's token efficiency without pre-grading.
- Batch-level uninformative-group resampling (DAPO-style) is complementary to bin-level sampling and likely stacks.

**Artifacts.** Sampler: MarinSkyRL `curriculum-sampling` @ 2a9034fd (checkpoint-resumable `data.sampling` subtree; worth PRing to main after multi-seed validation). Experiment: `experiments/post_training/curriculum_rl/` (PR to follow). Runs and curves: W&B project `marin-community/marin-curriculum-rl`; exported checkpoints under `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/users/power/checkpoints/curriculum-rl/<arm>/2026.08.29/exports/global_step_120`.

comments.author: rjpower
comments.body:
🤖 **Round 2 starting.** Scope, per review of round-1 results:

1. **DAPO dynamic sampling** — the pinned trainer already ships `trainer.algorithm.dynamic_sampling` (filter/replace with cross-batch accumulation); wiring it as arm variants (naive+dapo, thompson+dapo). One fix needed first: the curriculum-stat update must run before the filter, or every bin looks 100% informative to the sampler.
2. **Prior-sensitive pool** — round 1's grade-prior collapsed to thompson because 120 steps × 512 prompts of reward evidence swamps any prior over just 6 bins. Adding procedurally generated reasoning-gym bins (arithmetic chains, etc.) whose difficulty knobs give *genuine a-priori grades* and widen the bin count, so priors have room to matter. The reasoning-gym scorers only award 1.0 for a bare exact answer (full CoT responses get length-fuzz partial credit), so the env gets Minerva-style `Answer:`-line extraction first.
3. **Directional sampler** — new `learnability` kind: Thompson on per-bin pass rate, weight ∝ sampled p(1−p), which peaks at 50% solve rate and down-weights both all-pass and all-fail bins directionally (round-1 thompson treated them identically). `grade-prior` v2 seeds this posterior with grade-decreasing prior pass rates, so the prior is used directionally instead of as undirected optimism.
4. **Dropped:** grade-uniform (no signal over its simpler relatives in round 1).

Round-2 arms: naive, thompson, learnability, grade-prior(directional), grade-adaptive, naive+dapo, thompson+dapo — same fixed budgets and eval protocol as round 1.

comments.author: rjpower
comments.body:
🤖 **Round 2 infrastructure wired; smoke green.** All four follow-ups are implemented and validated end-to-end on cw-rno2a (`/power/curriculum-rl-r2-smoke2`):

- **DAPO** — `trainer.algorithm.dynamic_sampling.type=filter` wired as arm variants `naive-dapo` / `thompson-dapo`. The curriculum sampler now updates on **raw pre-filter batches** (MarinSkyRL `9a7286b4`); previously it would have run post-filter and read every bin as 100% informative. Smoke shows the filter engaging: 33–50/64 prompts informative per raw batch, one resample batch per step.
- **Prior-sensitive datasets** — pool v3 adds seven procedurally generated reasoning-gym bins (chain_sum ×3, spell_backward ×2, base_conversion ×2; 1,200 rows each) whose difficulty knobs give genuine a-priori grades, interleaved with the re-graded math bins on a shared 0–10 scale. The `reasoning_gym` env scores only the final `Answer:` line (`d36ceaaa`) — full CoT responses previously got ~0.05 fuzz credit even when correct. Smoke pass rates confirm the machinery and expose grade-placement surprises to analyze at full scale (chain_sum-med ~0.9 at grade 3; spell-backward ~0.15–0.33 vs math-l12 ~0.03 — spelling is easier for the base model than its grade assumed).
- **Directional sampler** — new `learnability` kind: Thompson draw on each bin's decayed pass rate, weighted by p·(1−p), peaking at 50% solve rate so it distinguishes too-easy from too-hard (the informative-group signal alone cannot). `grade-prior` is redefined as its grade-seeded variant: prior pass-rate mean falls linearly from 0.85 (easiest grade) to 0.05 (hardest) with pseudo-count `grade_prior_strength` (`0b44138c`).
- **Grade-uniform dropped** from the arm catalog.

Launching round-2 full arms next: naive, thompson, learnability, grade-adaptive, grade-prior, naive-dapo, thompson-dapo — 120 steps × 64 H100s each on the expanded pool.
